citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For the type set $\mathcal G$ and cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], define the relation $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ by $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')=F(\Gamma',\Gamma)=0$. Let $\mathcal P:=\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$ be the set of raw type pairs. Define a relation on raw pairs by

$$(A,B)\equiv(A',B')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists C\text{ such that }A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C.$$

The separate well-definedness lemma proves that $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with composition and positive scaling, that $\equiv$ is an equivalence on $\mathcal P$, and that the following operations are well-defined on its classes. After that proof, write $V_F:=\mathcal P/\equiv$. Define addition by $[(A,B)]+[(D,E)]:=[(A\times D,B\times E)]$, negation by $-[(A,B)]:=[(B,A)]$, and positive scaling by $t[(A,B)]:=[(tA,tB)]$. Set zero to $[(1,1)]$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. The same lemma establishes that these operations make $V_F$ a real vector space; no vector-space law is assumed by this Definition.

For the construction in [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]], $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling; $V_F$ is a real vector space and its displayed operations are representative-independent.

For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $V$ be a real vector space and $p:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p(0)=0$, $p(tx)=tp(x)$ for every $t>0$, and $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)$ in extended-real arithmetic. Assume **no sinks**: $p(x)<+\infty$ if and only if $p(-x)<+\infty$. Put $W:=\{x\in V:p(x)<+\infty\}$. Then $W$ is a linear subspace and there exists a real-linear $L:V\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$-p(-x)\le L(x)\le p(x)\qquad(x\in V),$$

with $-\infty\le r\le+\infty$ interpreted in the usual extended order. The result is valid in arbitrary dimension and allows $p=+\infty$ outside $W$.

For the conditional offset application, let $V=V_{\mathcal G}$ from [[def-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space]], let $F:\mathcal G\times\mathcal G\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p([e_\Gamma]-[e_{\Gamma'}])=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, and define $B(\Gamma):=L([e_\Gamma])$. Then $B(\Gamma\times\Gamma')=B(\Gamma)+B(\Gamma')$, $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$, and

$$-F(\Gamma',\Gamma)\le B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma').$$

For each $\Gamma\in\mathcal G$, let $X_\Gamma$ be a state set and $\sigma_\Gamma:X_\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ a baseline state function. If every admitted transition $(\Gamma,x)\to(\Gamma',y)$, with $x\in X_\Gamma$ and $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$, satisfies $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, then $\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)$ is nondecreasing across those transitions. The existence or properties of such a cost $p$, including no-sinks, are hypotheses and are not proved by this theorem.

Assume the calibrated entropy family of [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]], the cross-type accessibility axioms A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and the decorated cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]. For every pair of types $\Gamma,\Gamma'$ and states $x\in X_\Gamma$, $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$,

$$x\prec y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_\Gamma(x)+F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le \sigma_{\Gamma'}(y).$$

The infimum defining $F$ need not be attained. If $F=+\infty$, the right side is false; if $F=-\infty$, the right side is true.

derivations.claim: If $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty$, no-sinks gives a finite reverse witness of some real cost $c$. Concatenating it with any forward witness makes a closed chain, so [F2] gives forward cost at least $-c$. Thus $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')>-\infty$ whenever it is finite; all cost values are in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$.

For a pair class $v=[\Gamma,\Gamma']\in V_F$, define $p(v):=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Suppose $(\Gamma,\Gamma')\equiv(\Lambda,\Lambda')$ via $C$, so $P=\Gamma\times\Lambda'\times C\approx_0 Q=\Lambda\times\Gamma'\times C$. Put $D=\Gamma'\times\Lambda'\times C$. Since $P\approx_0 Q$, the triangle inequality gives $F(P,D)\le F(Q,D)$ and $F(Q,D)\le F(P,D)$; the costs have no $-\infty$ by step 1.1, so these inequalities imply equality. Catalyst invariance from [F2] gives $F(P,D)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ and $F(Q,D)=F(\Lambda,\Lambda')$. Therefore $p$ is independent of the pair representative.

The identity $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$ gives $p(0)=0$. Homogeneity of $F$ gives $p(tv)=tp(v)$ for $t>0$, and its product subadditivity gives $p(v+w)\le p(v)+p(w)$. The no-sinks condition says $p(v)<+\infty$ exactly when $p(-v)<+\infty$. By step 1.1, $p$ has no $-\infty$ value.

Apply [F3] to $V_F$ and $p$. It gives a real-linear $L:V_F\to\mathbb R$ with $-p(-v)\le L(v)\le p(v)$ for all $v$. Put $B(\Gamma)=L([\Gamma,1])$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. Since $[\Gamma\times\Gamma',1]=[\Gamma,1]+[\Gamma',1]$, $B$ is additive. Since $[t\Gamma,1]=t[\Gamma,1]$ (the unit type satisfies $t1=1$), $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$. Also $[\Gamma,\Gamma']=[\Gamma,1]-[\Gamma',1]$, so applying the sandwich to this pair gives the displayed two-sided cost bound.

For an admitted transition, [F4] gives $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, while step 3.1 gives $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Subtracting the latter from the former yields
$[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)+B(\Gamma')]-[\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)]\ge0.$
Thus the offset entropy is nondecreasing across every admitted transition.

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\iota_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\iota_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\iota(x):=\iota_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\iota_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\iota_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\iota_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\iota_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\iota_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\iota_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\iota_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\iota_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\iota_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\iota_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\iota_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\iota_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\iota_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\iota_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Let $I$ be a nonempty set of primitive simple-system labels containing a distinguished meter label $m$. Assume every finite separated product is explicitly represented by its finitely many tagged elementary factors; positive scaling and finite product are the only identifications. Suppose the join-closed family satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]], and fix a strict meter pair $z_0\prec\prec z_1$ in $\Gamma_m$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Then one can choose, for every $i\in I$, an additive constant and positive scale for its same-type entropy so that

$$S\big((t_1i_1,x_1),\ldots,(t_ni_n,x_n)\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^n t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$$

is additive, extensive, and characterizes every same-composition comparison on every finite separated product. No conclusion is asserted for transitions that change composition.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of tagged system types closed under finite composition $T\times T'$ and positive scaling $tT$. Scaling is associative and acts componentwise on products: $s(tT)=(st)T$ and $t(T\times T')=(tT)\times(tT')$. Each type $T$ has a nonempty state set $X_T$ of finite tagged compounds, every state in $X_T$ is represented by the coefficient-map interpretation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and has total coefficient mass $m(T)=w_T\ge0$, and $m(T\times T')=m(T)+m(T')$, $m(tT)=t\,m(T)$. The entropy $\sigma_T:X_T\to\mathbb R$ is the finite additive extensive entropy from [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]; in particular $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$.

Include the formal empty unit type $1$, with $X_1=\{*\}$, $m(1)=0$, $\sigma_1(*)=0$, $T\times1=T$, and $t1=1$. A transition edge from type $T$ to type $T'$ is a pair $a\in X_T$, $b\in X_{T'}$ such that the underlying equal-mass compounds satisfy $a\prec b$ under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Thus an edge can exist only when $m(T)=m(T')$. Its cost is the finite real number $\sigma_{T'}(b)-\sigma_T(a)$.

A decorated finite chain from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ consists of a catalyst type $C\in\mathcal G$, an integer $N\ge1$, types $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, and states $a_k\in X_{T_k}$, $b_{k+1}\in X_{T_{k+1}}$ with an edge $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$ for every $0\le k<N$. Its cost is the finite real sum

$$c=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\sigma_{T_{k+1}}(b_{k+1})-\sigma_{T_k}(a_k)\bigr).$$

Define $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ as the infimum of all such witness costs. Set $F=+\infty$ if there is no witness and $F=-\infty$ if the witness costs are unbounded below. The infimum is over real witness costs, so no subtraction of extended-real infima is used. Type permutations, reassociation, reversible identifications, and the identity $T\times1=T$ are part of the declared type structure. The cost identities and inequalities require a separate proof.

For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

derivations.claim: If $x\prec y$, the one-edge witness with an identity catalyst has cost $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$. Hence $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$, which is the forward inequality, including the case $F=+\infty$ where no such transition can exist.

Conversely assume the displayed entropy inequality. It is impossible when $F=+\infty$. For each integer $n\ge1$, choose a decorated witness of real cost $c_n\le\Delta\sigma+h/n$, where $\Delta\sigma=\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$ and $h=\sigma(z_1)-\sigma(z_0)>0$ is the entropy gap of a fixed strict meter pair from [F1]. Such witnesses exist from the definition of infimum, also if $F=-\infty$. Write their types as $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, their edges as $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$, and their endpoints as $a_0=(\widetilde x,c_0)$, $b_N=(\widetilde y,d_0)$.

Put $\delta_n=1/n$. In one finite compound type form
$L_n=(x,b_N,b_1,\ldots,b_{N-1},\delta_n z_0),\qquad R_n=(a_0,y,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1},\delta_n z_1).$
These have the same composition: both contain $\Gamma$, $\Gamma'$, the catalyst $C$, every intermediate type $T_1,\ldots,T_{N-1}$, and one scaled meter state, up to reassociation and permutation. Additivity of $\sigma$ and the definition of chain cost give
$\sigma(R_n)-\sigma(L_n)=\Delta\sigma-c_n+\delta_n h\ge0.$
Thus the same-composition entropy representation [F1] gives $L_n\prec R_n$.

Starting from $R_n$, use consistency on $a_0\prec b_1$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators. The result contains $b_1$ in place of $a_0$. Next use $a_1\prec b_2$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,b_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators, and continue in order. At stage $k$, the current compound contains $a_k$, the earlier outputs $b_1,\ldots,b_k$, all later inputs $a_{k+1},\ldots,a_{N-1}$, and the unchanged $y,\delta_nz_1$. After the last edge, transitivity gives $R_n\prec R'_n$, where $R'_n=(b_1,\ldots,b_N,y,\delta_nz_1)$. Compose this with $L_n\prec R_n$ from step 2.1. The compounds $L_n$ and $R'_n$ share the finite spectator $b_1+\cdots+b_N$; cancel it by [F4]. The result is $x+\delta_nz_0\prec y+\delta_nz_1$ for every $n$.

Since $\delta_n\downarrow0$, stability in [A1] with bases $x,y$ and fixed positive spectators $z_0,z_1$ yields $x\prec y$. This proves the reverse implication without assuming that any infimum is attained.

Fix a family $I$ of primitive material labels. A tagged type $c\in I$ retains its identity even if another type has the same coordinate domain. A positive scale $\lambda>0$ is dimensionless and is represented by the separately tagged bulk copy $c^{(\lambda)}$ and map $\delta_\lambda$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A finite separated compound is a finite tuple of tagged scaled systems, with permutation and reassociation identifications and an empty unit type. Its state is a tuple of constituent equilibrium states; its extensive coordinate tuple is the sum specified by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] whenever the pair is admitted there.

The formal composition vector of a compound records, for each primitive label $c$, the sum of its positive scale coefficients. Two compounds have the same composition exactly when these vectors agree. The distinct **formal mass** $m(A)$ is the sum of all scale coefficients in $A$, a dimensionless bookkeeping quantity; it is not physical mass in kilograms, mole amount, energy, or volume. Same-composition compounds have equal formal mass. For states $A,B$ of the same compound type, write $A\prec B$ when the declared adiabatic-accessibility relation of [[def-td-adiabatic-accessibility]] admits that endpoint comparison. This definition does not infer accessibility from coordinate addition.

An equal-composition comparison is a comparison between states of types with the same formal composition vector. The later reaction-network definition may separately admit transitions between distinct composition types, but the mathematical supplier still requires equal formal mass at both endpoints. A physical application must state how its channel preserves the chosen formal mass and separately record its dimensioned conservation balances. The empty unit has one state and formal mass zero. No identity is imposed between a primitive type and a scaled tag, or between two different decompositions of a compound, beyond the explicitly declared reassociation, permutation, and bulk-composition maps.

Use thermal joins and $\sim_T$ exactly as defined in [[def-td-thermal-join]]. For every ordered pair of simple systems and every admitted finite join, adopt:

**T1 (joining).** $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$.

**T2 (reversible splitting).** Every join state has at least one split into component states at its stated total energy and work coordinates that is reversible to the join state. Also, for every state $x$ and every $0<t<1$, the equal-state scaled split $(t x,(1-t)x)$ is reversible to $x$.

**T3 (thermal-equilibrium transitivity).** If $x\sim_T y$ and $y\sim_T z$ in the model’s declared contact family, then $x\sim_T z$. This requires the model to provide the relevant joined types and identifications.

**T4 (transversality).** For each simple-system state $x$, there are $x_0,x_1$ in that system with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$.

The axioms apply to admitted types and their joins only. T4 is an assumption about the contact relation; it is not a consequence of an equation of state or of a thermometer reading. The stronger range condition T5 is stated separately in [[post-td-universal-thermal-range]], and join coherence C1 is separately stated in [[post-td-equilibrium-join-coherence]].

derivations.claim: Start at $(1,3)$. Then $\bar U=2$, every point of $A$ has second coordinate at least $3$, and every point of $B$ has second coordinate at least $2$. A finite convex combination of points whose second coordinates are at least $2$ still has second coordinate at least $2$, because it is the weighted sum of those coordinates with nonnegative weights summing to one. Hence every point in $\operatorname{conv}(A\cup B)$ has second coordinate at least $2$, so $(3,1)$ is not in the forward sector and $(1,3)\not\prec(3,1)$.

In the one-system space, strict accessibility is exactly strict increase of $U$, while thermal equilibrium is equality of normalized energies. If $U_0\prec\prec U\prec\prec U_1$, then $U_0<U<U_1$, so $U_0\ne U_1$ and the two cannot be thermally equivalent. Thus T4 fails.

Start instead at $(3,1)$. Again $\bar U=2$; every point of its $A$ has first coordinate at least $3$, and every point of its $B$ has first coordinate at least $2$. Convex combinations therefore have first coordinate at least $2$, so $(1,3)$ is not accessible from $(3,1)$. The two product states are incomparable, and the comparison hypothesis fails.

The single-system function $S(U)=\log U$ is strictly increasing and represents $U\le U'$. If its additive sum represented product accessibility, the states $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$ would have equal summed entropy $\log 3$, forcing accessibility both ways. Step 1.1 and step 2.1 show neither direction holds. Therefore this single-system entropy does not represent the product relation. Since the example fails T4 by step 1.2, it does not satisfy the hypotheses of a product-comparison result that includes T4.

Let $A$ be a finite set of reaction channels, let $r\in\mathbb N$, let $\nu_a\in\mathbb R^r$ be the output-minus-input type vector of channel $a$, and let $d_a\in\mathbb R$ be a finite lower bound on its already calibrated entropy change. There exists an offset vector $b\in\mathbb R^r$ satisfying

$$b\cdot\nu_a+d_a\ge0\qquad(a\in A)$$

if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^A$ with $\lambda_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a\nu_a=0$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. If an actual transition has entropy change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, such a vector guarantees $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge0$. The criterion is exact for the finite lower-bound inequalities; it does not claim necessity for actual transitions when $d_a$ is only a loose bound.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ be finite, let $c_j\in\mathbb R^n$ and $h_j\in\mathbb R$ for $0\le j<m$. The finite system

$$c_j\cdot b\ge h_j\qquad(0\le j<m)$$

has a solution $b\in\mathbb R^n$ if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j=0$ satisfies $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jh_j\le0$. Dot products and sums are finite. This includes empty rows, empty variables, and an empty inequality family.

derivations.claim: The multiplier $\lambda=(1,1)$ is nonnegative and satisfies $\lambda_1\nu_1+\lambda_2\nu_2=(1,-1)+(-1,1)=(0,0)$. But $\lambda_1d_1+\lambda_2d_2=-2+1=-1<0$, violating the necessary condition in [F1]; therefore no offset exists.

Directly, the two inequalities would require $b_1-b_2\ge2$ and $-b_1+b_2\ge-1$, equivalently $b_1-b_2\le1$. Adding the original inequalities gives $0\ge1$, a contradiction. This is the positive-right-side zero-left certificate of [F2].

def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound.title: Tagged scalable compounds

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.A.1–II.A.2

def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound.statement:
Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined.title: Compound mass is well-defined and additive

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.A.1–II.A.2

lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined.statement: For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.
lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined.proof:
**Given:** [F1] and [F2].

1.1 Let $E$ be any finite subset of $X$ containing $\operatorname{supp}(c)$. On $E\setminus\operatorname{supp}(c)$ the function is zero, so the finite sum over $E$ equals the finite sum over $\operatorname{supp}(c)$ by [F2]. If $E$ and $E'$ both contain the support, compare each sum to the sum over the finite union $E\cup E'$; hence the value is independent of the chosen finite summation set. [F1, F2]

2.1 The support of $c+d$ is contained in the finite union of the supports of $c$ and $d$. Sum over that union; distributivity in [F2] gives $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$, since zero terms outside each individual support contribute nothing by step 1.1. The support of $tc$ equals that of $c$ for $t>0$, and scalar linearity of the finite sum gives $m(tc)=t m(c)$. For $t=0$, $tc=0$ and both $m(tc)$ and $t m(c)$ are zero. The empty sum is zero, so $m(0)=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The support of $e_x$ is the singleton $\{x\}$, whose one summand is $1$, so the recursion in [F2] gives $m(e_x)=0+1=1$. If $m(c)=0$, sum its nonnegative coefficients over its finite support. Clause 4 in [F2] forces every summand to be zero; coefficients off the support are also zero, hence $c=0$. Conversely $c=0$ has zero mass by step 2.1. Thus all the claimed mass identities hold, including the empty and unit-state cases. [F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

cor-tdmath-ordered-finite-mixture-envelo.title: Conditional finite-mixture envelope for an additive ordered representation
cor-tdmath-ordered-finite-mixture-envelo.statement: Assume the strict-reference representation conclusion of the draft supplier [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] for its nonempty state set $X$ and stated comparison hypotheses. For a finite nonempty list of distinct states $s_1,\ldots,s_m\in X$, let $e_s$ be the unit-state compound defined in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]; it is a mass-one point mass by [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]. For $\theta\in\Delta_m$, put $M_\theta=\sum_i\theta_i e_{s_i}$ and set $V(\theta):=\sum_i\theta_iS(s_i)$. Suppose a coordinate assignment $\chi$ on these compounds satisfies $\chi(M_\theta)=\sum_i\theta_iq_i$ for fixed $q_i\in\mathbb R^d$. For each $x$, define the value to be $+\infty$ if no $\theta\in\Delta_m$ has coordinate $x$. Then the minimum represented value among those finite mixtures, with that empty-feasible-set convention, is exactly the finite-mixture envelope $f_{\rm mix}(x)$ of [[thm-tdmath-finite-mixture-envelope]], with all its attainment, convexity, lower-semicontinuity, biconjugation, and supporting-face conclusions. This is the complete conditional transfer under the representation conclusion and affine coordinate assignment; the supplier definition and mass-one fact are provided locally.
cor-tdmath-ordered-finite-mixture-envelo.proof:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [A1] and [L1], each $a_i=S(s_i)$ is finite. For any $\theta\in\Delta_m$, [L2] gives $m(M_\theta)=\sum_i\theta_i m(e_{s_i})=\sum_i\theta_i=1$. If $\theta_i=0$, its term is the empty compound and contributes zero; equivalently omit such terms, leaving only positive coefficients and never applying a positive-scaling comparison axiom at zero. The representation assigns $M_\theta$ the value $V(\theta)=\sum_i\theta_i a_i$. By [A3], its coordinate is $\sum_i\theta_i q_i$. Since the states are distinct, the coefficient of $s_i$ in $M_\theta$ is exactly $\theta_i$, so this parametrization is injective. Hence mixtures in this fixed family with coordinate $x$ correspond exactly to $\theta\in\Theta_x$ from [L3]. [A1, A3, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

2.1 The minimum of $V(\theta)$ over those mixtures is therefore $\min_{\theta\in\Theta_x}\sum_i\theta_i a_i=f_{\rm mix}(x)$ by [L3], with $+\infty$ when $\Theta_x$ is empty. Every further conclusion in the Statement follows by applying the corresponding conclusion of [L3] to the same finite data. The point-mass and zero-coefficient cases are supplied by [L2]; the transfer remains conditional on [A1] and [A3] and records no independent acceptance of the draft representation. [A1, A3, L3, step 1.1] ∎

thm-tdmath-common-meter-calibration.title: Finite-family calibration by a common meter

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §II.E

thm-tdmath-common-meter-calibration.statement:
Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set of system types, $X_i$ a nonempty state set with chosen reference $r_i\in X_i$ for each $i\in I$, and $M$ a common meter state set with $z_0,z_1\in M$. Assume for every $i$ that the product state set $X_i\times M$ satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]], with strict reference pair $(r_i,z_0)\prec\prec(r_i,z_1)$. Let $S_i$ be its normalized representation and put $\sigma_i(x):=S_i(x,z_0)$. In that product comparison, the unit product-state point mass satisfies $e_{(x,z_0)}\sim_s(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{(r_i,z_0)}+\sigma_i(x)e_{(r_i,z_1)}$, by [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. These product-state point masses are distinct from the shared state-and-meter compounds defined next.

Assume in addition a **common-meter compatibility interface**. Let $\mathcal Y$ contain disjoint families of raw state tags $a_{i,x}$, raw type-reference tags $\rho_i$, and two distinct raw meter tags $\zeta_0,\zeta_1$. Using the unit point masses on these tags, write $e_{r_i}:=e_{\rho_i}$ and $e_{z_j}:=e_{\zeta_j}$, and define $u_{i,x}:=e_{a_{i,x}}+e_{z_0}$. Thus $u_{i,x}$ is an explicit mass-two state-and-fixed-meter compound; it is not a unit tag. Compounds over $\mathcal Y$ use the finite-support convention of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]], and their signed comparison is the one in [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]. Require the exact substitution

$$u_{i,x}\sim_s e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x)e_{z_1}\qquad(i\in I,\ x\in X_i),$$

finite substitutions to compose, and the fixed reference sum $\sum_iT_ie_{r_i}$ to cancel when type totals agree. Both sides of this signed substitution have total coefficient two, even when $\sigma_i(x)$ lies outside $[0,1]$. Require the common meter point masses to satisfy $e_{z_0}\preceq e_{z_1}$ and not $e_{z_1}\preceq e_{z_0}$. These are hypotheses on the comparison algebra, not consequences of separate numerical meter readings.

For positive coefficients $t_{ik}$ on a finite collection of type-$i$ states $x_{ik}$, define $T_i:=\sum_k t_{ik}$ and $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Put $C_0:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}e_{a_{i,x_{ik}}}$ and $C:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}u_{i,x_{ik}}=C_0+T e_{z_0}$. Thus $C_0$ is the state compound of mass $T$ and $C$ is its fixed-meter encoding of mass $2T$. Empty collections give $T=0$ and $C_0=C=0$. Define

$$\Sigma(C):=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_k t_{ik}\sigma_i(x_{ik}).$$

For two such compounds $C,D$ with the same type-total vector $(T_i)_{i\in I}$, the common comparison satisfies $C\preceq D$ exactly when $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Equivalently, the same order criterion holds for the state compounds $C_0,D_0$ after canceling their common $T e_{z_0}$. The index family is finite; no arbitrary-index choice or infinite decomposition is asserted.
thm-tdmath-common-meter-calibration.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 For each constituent $(i,x_{ik},z_0)$ of $C$, its mass-two shared compound $u_{i,x_{ik}}$ is equivalent by the exact substitution in [A1] to $e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x_{ik}))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x_{ik})e_{z_1}$. Each side has total coefficient two, so this signed substitution is defined. Scale by $t_{ik}>0$ and combine the finitely many comparisons using [A1] and [F2]. The resulting reference-system part is $\sum_iT_i e_{r_i}$, independent of the chosen states. The meter part has coefficients $T-\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_0}$ and $\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_1}$, where $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Hence $C$ is equivalent to that fixed reference-system compound plus $(T-\Sigma(C))e_{z_0}+\Sigma(C)e_{z_1}$, whose total coefficient is $T+T=2T$. If the collection is empty, both expressions are zero and the equivalence is reflexivity, requiring no order scaling at zero. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The same substitution for $D$ gives the same reference-system compound because its type totals are the same, and the same total meter mass $T$. Cancel the common reference-system terms by [A1] and [F2]. If $T>0$, the remaining meter expressions have total coefficient $T$; positive scaling by $1/T$ turns them into the unit reference maps $R_{\Sigma(C)/T}$ and $R_{\Sigma(D)/T}$. By [F3] these compare exactly when $\Sigma(C)/T\le\Sigma(D)/T$, which is equivalent to $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Scaling back by $T>0$ proves the reverse comparison equivalence, so no unit-mass reference theorem is applied directly at mass $T$. Reversing the same equivalences proves the converse implication as well. Since $C=C_0+T e_{z_0}$ and $D=D_0+T e_{z_0}$, [F2] also gives $C\preceq D$ exactly when $C_0\preceq D_0$; for $T=0$ all these compounds are empty and the criterion is $0\le0$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

ex-tdmath-common-meter-two-types.title: Two types on one meter scale

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §II.E

ex-tdmath-common-meter-two-types.proof:
**Given:** [A1], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 Both compounds have type-total vector $(1,1)$, so [F1] applies. Their calibrated values are $\Sigma(C)=1+1/3=4/3$ and $\Sigma(D)=0+3=3$. Since $4/3\le3$, [F1] gives $C\preceq D$. The theorem also cancels their common $2e_{z_0}$, giving $C_0\preceq D_0$. The value $3$ is permitted by [F2]; the representation theorem imposes no unit-interval bound on arbitrary states. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Reversing the comparison would require $3\le4/3$, which is false; hence this particular comparison is strict. No separate per-type numerical reading is treated as a proof of common-meter compatibility; that remains the stated hypothesis. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses.title: Forward-sector hypotheses for a simple state domain

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§III.A–III.B
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses.statement:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\iota_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\iota_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\iota(x):=\iota_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\iota_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\iota_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\iota_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\iota_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\iota_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\iota_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\iota_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\iota_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\iota_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\iota_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\iota_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\iota_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\iota_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\iota_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses.title: Thermal joins and conditional contact hypotheses

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §IV.A, pp. 51–54
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses.statement:
For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\iota_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\iota_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\iota_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\iota_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\iota_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\iota_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellatio.title: Spectator cancellation without comparison completeness

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 2.1 and §III.C
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.1 and 7.2–7.3, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellatio.statement: Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.
lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellatio.proof:
1.1 Assume $A+C\prec B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\prec B/n+C/n$. Define $E_j=(n-j)A/n+jB/n+C/n$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$. For $j<n$, add the common spectator $(n-j-1)A/n+jB/n$ to the scaled comparison to obtain $E_j\prec E_{j+1}$. Transitivity yields $A+C/n=E_0\prec E_n=B+C/n$. Stability with bases $A,B$, fixed positive spectators $C,C$, and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ gives $A\prec B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity gives $C=0$ and the implication is immediate. Conversely, consistency gives $A+C\prec B+C$ from $A\prec B$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For equal-total signed maps $u,v$, the difference $d=v-u$ has finite support and total coefficient zero, so $m(d^+)=m(d^-)$. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, their pointwise common part $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$ gives $u=k+d^-$ and $v=k+d^+$. Cancellation in step 1.1 proves $u\prec v$ exactly when $d^-\prec d^+$, which by [F2] is $u\preceq_s v$; adding a common signed map leaves $d$ unchanged by [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, [F2] identifies these with comparisons of $(v-u)^-$ to $(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-$ to $(w-v)^+$. Consistency combines them. Their pointwise common minimum cancels by step 1.1, leaving $(w-u)^-\prec(w-u)^+$, which [F2] identifies as $u\preceq_s w$. The same finite-sum argument proves closure under addition; reflexivity follows from reflexivity of the zero compound. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

cex-tdmath-bare-contact-interface-incohe.title: The bare join coordinates do not determine contact coherence

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §IV.A, pp. 51–54
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapter 4, complete 607-page edition

cex-tdmath-bare-contact-interface-incohe.statement: The coordinate set formula for a thermal join, without an accessibility or thermal-equilibrium specification, forces C1 join coherence.
cex-tdmath-bare-contact-interface-incohe.proof:
1.1 Take one simple coordinate set $\Gamma=\mathbb R^2$ and a distinct tagged join set
$\Delta=\{(u,v_1,v_2):\exists u_1,u_2\in\mathbb R,\ u=u_1+u_2\}=\mathbb R^3.$
For tagged states $x=(u_1,v_1)$ and $y=(u_2,v_2)$, define $J(x,y)=(u_1+u_2,v_1,v_2)$. This satisfies the stated set-level coordinate formula. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 On the disjoint tagged union $S=\Gamma\sqcup\Delta$, interpret an otherwise unconstrained relation symbol $\sim_T$ as equality. It is an equivalence relation. For any $x\in\Gamma$, $x\sim_T x$, but $J(x,x)\in\Delta$ is a distinct tagged object and hence $J(x,x)\not\sim_T x$. Thus C1 fails while the coordinate formula remains satisfied. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On the same tagged sets, interpreting $\sim_T$ as the universal relation instead makes C1 true, without changing $\Gamma$, $\Delta$, or $J$. The bare coordinate data therefore do not determine C1. These interpretations are countermodels only to the stated set-data implication; they are not claimed to satisfy T1–T5. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

def-td-cross-type-reaction-network.title: Cross-type mixing and reaction network

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§VI.A–VI.B

def-td-cross-type-reaction-network.statement:
A cross-type mixing and reaction network consists of a declared set $\mathcal G$ of tagged composition types, a state set $X_\Gamma$ for each $\Gamma\in\mathcal G$, and a set of channel-labelled process records. A record $P$ for a channel $\alpha$ has an equilibrium initial state $x^-_P\in X_\Gamma$, an equilibrium final state $x^+_P\in X_{\Gamma'}$, and the full protocol, outer-boundary, energy and auxiliary data needed for that channel. The channel declares its own dimensioned material-balance constraints and whether heat or work crosses the outer boundary; the fixed-composition record type of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]] is recovered when $\Gamma=\Gamma'$. Define $(\Gamma,x)\mathcal R(\Gamma',y)$ exactly when at least one admitted channel record has those endpoint states. No channel is inferred from separated composition.

For any permitted equal-formal-mass compound states $A,B$ of the network, define $A\prec B$ exactly when at least one admitted channel record has initial state $A$ and final state $B$; for named single types this is the relation $\mathcal R$ above. This is the exact relation supplied to [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], not a separate abstract order that enlarges or restricts the channel edges. Its extension to finite tagged products and common spectators is governed by the adopted A1–A6 conditions below. Thus every edge in a decorated chain is precisely an admitted channel transition. This identification is a declared model condition.

The network is **finite-factor closed** when its types admit the declared finite composition and positive scaling operations and each allowed channel respects the model’s stated conservation constraints. In addition, each channel must preserve the dimensionless formal mass $m$ of [[def-td-scaled-products-and-comparison]]; this is the equal-coefficient-mass convention required by the mathematical chain-cost supplier, not a statement that formal mass is kilograms or moles. The common relation on all equal-formal-mass compounds satisfies A1–A6 of [[post-td-accessibility-a1-a6]], including consistency with spectators and stability. A decorated finite chain is exactly a finite sequence of such allowed transitions with a common catalyst and the real baseline-entropy edge costs in [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]].

For $\Gamma,\Gamma'$, let $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ be the infimum of those finite decorated-chain costs, with $+\infty$ if no witness exists and $-\infty$ if costs are unbounded below. The network has **no sinks** when, for every ordered type pair,

$$F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F(\Gamma',\Gamma)<+\infty.$$

No-sinks is an explicit property required of a network used in the global-offset theorem; it is not proved by this definition, and it is not asserted for every physical mixing or reaction. The definition permits the channel set to be empty; then the condition must still be checked rather than inferred.
def-td-cross-type-reaction-network.physical_scope: A declared family of allowed transitions between distinct tagged composition types, with finite catalyst chains and an explicit no-sinks condition; this definition does not claim a particular material network satisfies it.

def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability.title: Comparison and stability for compounds

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.C–II.D
Campión et al., A Survey on the Mathematical Foundations of Axiomatic Entropy, §§2–5

def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability.statement:
Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space.title: Cost-zero type offsets and their difference space

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B, pp. 76–79
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space.statement:
For the type set $\mathcal G$ and cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], define the relation $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ by $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')=F(\Gamma',\Gamma)=0$. Let $\mathcal P:=\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$ be the set of raw type pairs. Define a relation on raw pairs by

$$(A,B)\equiv(A',B')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists C\text{ such that }A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C.$$

The separate well-definedness lemma proves that $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with composition and positive scaling, that $\equiv$ is an equivalence on $\mathcal P$, and that the following operations are well-defined on its classes. After that proof, write $V_F:=\mathcal P/\equiv$. Define addition by $[(A,B)]+[(D,E)]:=[(A\times D,B\times E)]$, negation by $-[(A,B)]:=[(B,A)]$, and positive scaling by $t[(A,B)]:=[(tA,tB)]$. Set zero to $[(1,1)]$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. The same lemma establishes that these operations make $V_F$ a real vector space; no vector-space law is assumed by this Definition.

def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs.title: Decorated finite-chain costs with catalysts

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B, Eqs. 6.6, 6.9, and 6.10, pp. 74–75
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs.statement:
Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of tagged system types closed under finite composition $T\times T'$ and positive scaling $tT$. Scaling is associative and acts componentwise on products: $s(tT)=(st)T$ and $t(T\times T')=(tT)\times(tT')$. Each type $T$ has a nonempty state set $X_T$ of finite tagged compounds, every state in $X_T$ is represented by the coefficient-map interpretation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and has total coefficient mass $m(T)=w_T\ge0$, and $m(T\times T')=m(T)+m(T')$, $m(tT)=t\,m(T)$. The entropy $\sigma_T:X_T\to\mathbb R$ is the finite additive extensive entropy from [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]; in particular $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$.

Include the formal empty unit type $1$, with $X_1=\{*\}$, $m(1)=0$, $\sigma_1(*)=0$, $T\times1=T$, and $t1=1$. A transition edge from type $T$ to type $T'$ is a pair $a\in X_T$, $b\in X_{T'}$ such that the underlying equal-mass compounds satisfy $a\prec b$ under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Thus an edge can exist only when $m(T)=m(T')$. Its cost is the finite real number $\sigma_{T'}(b)-\sigma_T(a)$.

A decorated finite chain from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ consists of a catalyst type $C\in\mathcal G$, an integer $N\ge1$, types $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, and states $a_k\in X_{T_k}$, $b_{k+1}\in X_{T_{k+1}}$ with an edge $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$ for every $0\le k<N$. Its cost is the finite real sum

$$c=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\sigma_{T_{k+1}}(b_{k+1})-\sigma_{T_k}(a_k)\bigr).$$

Define $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ as the infimum of all such witness costs. Set $F=+\infty$ if there is no witness and $F=-\infty$ if the witness costs are unbounded below. The infimum is over real witness costs, so no subtraction of extended-real infima is used. Type permutations, reassociation, reversible identifications, and the identity $T\times1=T$ are part of the declared type structure. The cost identities and inequalities require a separate proof.

def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison.title: Signed comparison for forward-sector relations

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §II.D
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §4.1, complete 607-page edition

def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison.statement: Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\iota(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

def-tdmath-signed-comparison.title: Signed comparison of finite coefficient maps

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §II.D

def-tdmath-signed-comparison.statement:
Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

ex-tdmath-logarithmic-coherence-witness.title: Logarithmic contact model with coherent joins

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§III–IV, pp. 37–59
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

ex-tdmath-logarithmic-coherence-witness.proof:
**Given:** The formulas and definitions in the Example, with all $c_i,r_i,u_i^*,v_i^*>0$.

1.1 Fix a finite list of scaled components with amounts $t_j>0$ and labels $i_j\in I$. Write $\alpha_j=t_jc_{i_j}$, $\beta_j=t_jr_{i_j}$, $d_j=t_ju^*_{i_j}$, and $e_j=t_jv^*_{i_j}$, with $C=\sum_j\alpha_j>0$. For a split of total energy $U>0$ into positive $U_j$ with $\sum_jU_j=U$, put $p_j=\alpha_j/C$ and $r_j=U_j/\alpha_j$. Then $\sum_jp_jr_j=U/C$. By [F5] and monotonicity of $\log$ from [F3],
$\sum_j\alpha_j\log(U_j/d_j)
=\sum_j\alpha_j\log(\alpha_j/d_j)+C\sum_jp_j\log r_j
\le \sum_j\alpha_j\log(\alpha_j/d_j)+C\log(U/C)
=\sum_j\alpha_j\log(\alpha_jU/(Cd_j)).$
Equality in the finite weighted Jensen step occurs only when all $r_j$ are equal: [F6] gives strict concavity for any unequal pair with positive weights, and grouping terms applies this two-point strict inequality inductively. Since the weighted average is $U/C$, equality requires $r_j=U/C$, or $U_j=\alpha_jU/C$. This allocation is positive and feasible, so the maximum is attained uniquely. The work-coordinate terms do not depend on the energy split, giving exactly the displayed join entropy. Grouping nested joins is the same finite maximization over all $U_j$, so the formula is associative under grouping and permutation. [F2, F3, F5, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 On each fixed composition, define accessibility by nondecrease of the displayed entropy. Reflexivity and transitivity follow from the real order. A common spectator adds the same entropy to both sides; positive scaling multiplies each entropy comparison by a positive factor. For a simple scaled type, replacing $(U,V,t)$ by $(sU,sV,st)$ leaves both log ratios unchanged and multiplies their coefficients and constant term by $s$. In a join, scaling every amount, energy, and work coordinate by $s$ likewise leaves $\alpha_jU/(Cd_j)$ and $V_j/e_j$ unchanged and scales all coefficients and additive constants by $s$. Extensivity gives $\sigma_{(s+t)i}((s+t)x)=\sigma_{si}(sx)+\sigma_{ti}(tx)$, proving reversible splitting. For the stability condition, if $\sigma(A)+\epsilon_n\sigma(Z_0)\le\sigma(B)+\epsilon_n\sigma(Z_1)$ for all $n$ and $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$, the four entropies are finite. Moreover, the premise includes equality of aggregate composition: $\nu(A)-\nu(B)=\epsilon_n(\nu(Z_1)-\nu(Z_0))$ for every $n$. Choose two different values of $\epsilon_n$, which exist because the positive sequence tends to zero; subtracting these equalities gives $\nu(Z_1)=\nu(Z_0)$, and then $\nu(A)=\nu(B)$. Taking limits in the entropy inequality gives $\sigma(A)\le\sigma(B)$, now with the same-composition condition required by the accessibility definition. This verifies the stated accessibility and stability hypotheses on the declared comparison domains. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.3 For $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, strict concavity of $\log$ from [F6] gives concavity of $(U,V)\mapsto c_i\log(U/u_i^*)+r_i\log(V/v_i^*)$. Jensen's inequality in each coordinate yields $t\sigma_i(x)+(1-t)\sigma_i(y)\le\sigma_i(tx+(1-t)y)$, so the convex-combination access condition in [F1] holds. Strict increase of $\log U$ at fixed $V$ gives a strict successor, proving S1. [F1, F3, F4, F6, given, algebra]

1.4 For a simple type of amount $t$, put $\alpha=tc_i$ and $\beta=tr_i$. Its forward sector is the superlevel set of $\alpha\log U+\beta\log V$; the boundary through $(U_0,V_0)$ is the smooth graph $U=U_0(V/V_0)^{-\beta/\alpha}$ for $V>0$. By [F4], its tangent slope is $dU/dV=-\beta U/(\alpha V)$, so the support plane has the required form with $P(U,V)=\beta U/(\alpha V)$. The gradient is nonzero. For any boundary tangent vector, a differentiable boundary curve exists with that tangent; applying a supporting linear inequality to both positive and negative curve parameters forces the support normal to annihilate the tangent space. That space has codimension one and its normal is the nonzero gradient, so the supporting hyperplane is unique. The slope $P$ is smooth and locally Lipschitz. The graph domain $(0,\infty)$ is arcwise connected, proving S2–S3. For a finite join, replace $\alpha$ by $C$ and use each positive $\beta_j$; the boundary graph $U=K\prod_jV_j^{-\beta_j/C}$ lies over the connected positive orthant and has locally Lipschitz slopes $P_j=\beta_jU/(CV_j)$. [F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.5 For any state $(U,V)$ of amount $t$ and any allowed work coordinate $W>0$ in a second type of amount $t'$, choose $Y=(t'c_jU/(tc_i),W)$. It lies in the positive state domain and satisfies $\theta_{ti}(U,V)=\theta_{t'j}(Y)$, verifying T5. For T4, choose $0<V_0<V<V_1$ at fixed $U$. Strict increase in the volume coordinate gives $(U,V_0)\prec\prec(U,V)\prec\prec(U,V_1)$, while the endpoints have the same $\theta=U/(tc_i)$ and hence are thermally equivalent. [F1, F2, F3, given, choose]

2.1 Step 1.1 shows that joined entropy is the maximum of the separated entropy over all admissible energy splits. Thus every split compares upward to the join, and the maximizing split has equal entropy with the join, so it compares back; this verifies T1–T2. For a pair of simple components, the maximizing allocation is characterized by $U_i/\alpha_i=U_j/\alpha_j$, exactly equality of $\theta_{t_i i}(U_i,V_i):=U_i/(t_ic_i)$ and $\theta_{t_j j}(U_j,V_j)$. The initial split is reversible with the join exactly when its entropy equals the maximum, which is exactly this equality. Therefore $\sim_T$ is equality of the scalar label, and transitivity follows. [F1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, given]

3.1 If two component states are thermally equivalent, their common label is $\theta$. At their join, the maximizing split has energies $U_i=t_ic_i\theta$ and $U_j=t_jc_j\theta$, so the joined label is $(U_i+U_j)/(t_ic_i+t_jc_j)=\theta$. The same identity holds after any finite grouping by step 1.1. Therefore the joined state is thermally equivalent to each component, verifying C1 under the declared nested-join identifications. Every logarithm argument is a ratio of like positive quantities, hence dimensionless. The parameter $\theta$ is only a mathematical contact label; this example asserts no empirical temperature law. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

ex-tdmath-reference-order-two-state.title: Two-state reference order

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Lemma 2.2

ex-tdmath-reference-order-two-state.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and $a,b$ as distinct tags.

1.1 Reflexivity and transitivity follow from those properties of $\le$ on the $b$ coefficient, and CH follows because $\le$ is total. Adding a common compound adds the same $b$ coefficient to each side, so consistency holds. Multiplying both coefficients by $t>0$ preserves the inequality. Splitting a state coefficient into two positive parts preserves the total coefficient of $b$, so splitting/recombination gives equivalence. Finally $e_a\preceq e_b$ because $0\le1$, while $e_b\npreceq e_a$ because $1\nleq0$. [A1, F1]

1.2 For stability, suppose $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, with $\epsilon_n\to0$ and fixed positive $Z_0,Z_1$. If $A(b)>B(b)$, let $\delta=A(b)-B(b)>0$ and $q:=|Z_0(b)-Z_1(b)|$. If $q=0$, every perturbed difference remains $\delta>0$; if $q>0$, choose $n$ with $\epsilon_n q<\delta$. In either case some perturbed $b$-coefficient difference is positive, contradicting the assumed comparison. Thus $A(b)\le B(b)$, which is $A\preceq B$. [A1, F1]

2.1 The reference pair $x_0=a,x_1=b$ is strict by step 1.1. Therefore [F2] applies and yields $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$ iff $\lambda\le\mu$ for all real $\lambda,\mu$, including parameters outside $[0,1]$. The signed parameters are handled by the signed comparison definition, not by treating $R_\lambda$ as a nonnegative compound. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

lem-tdmath-contact-energy-orientation.title: Thermal joins force a common mathematical energy orientation

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, single-system energy orientation and thermal-contact axioms, §§III–IV; the common-sign deduction is supplied locally

lem-tdmath-contact-energy-orientation.statement: Let a family of simple domains satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and suppose every pair has an admitted simple thermal join satisfying T1 and T2 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then the fixed-work orientation signs from [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]] agree throughout the family. One common affine proof-coordinate convention $u'=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, therefore makes each fixed-work accessibility order increase with $u'$ and preserves the energy-sum formula for joins. This is a mathematical coordinate convention; it does not change a physical energy quantity or assert a sign of a measured temperature.
lem-tdmath-contact-energy-orientation.proof:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 Suppose two component signs are opposed. Choose a join state $Z$ and a reversible split $(x,y)$ by T2 in [A2]. Write $x=(u_x,v_x)$ and $y=(u_y,v_y)$. Openness in [A1] permits a sufficiently small nonzero $\delta$ with $x'=(u_x+\delta,v_x)$ and $y'=(u_y-\delta,v_y)$ in their respective charts. Choose the sign of $\delta$ so $\varepsilon_{\Gamma_x}\delta>0$; opposed signs imply $\varepsilon_{\Gamma_y}(-\delta)>0$. Thus [F1] gives $x\prec\prec x'$ and $y\prec\prec y'$. These pairs have the same summed energy and work coordinates and the same represented aggregate composition and mass. [A1, A2, F1, construct]

2.1 If $(x',y')\prec(x,y)$, consistency with $y\prec y'$ gives $(x',y)\prec(x',y')\prec(x,y)$. Cancel the common represented spectator $y$ by [F2] to get $x'\prec x$, contrary to step 1.1. But T1 gives $(x',y')\prec Z$, and the chosen T2 split gives $Z\prec(x,y)$, so transitivity produces exactly this forbidden reverse comparison. Opposed signs are impossible. Every pair has an admitted join, hence one common sign $\varepsilon$ works for the whole family. The affine change $u'=\varepsilon u$ preserves openness and convexity and sends $u=u_x+u_y$ to $u'=\varepsilon u_x+\varepsilon u_y$; its positive orientation describes the same accessibility relation. No physical energy, unit or calibration premise is redefined. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness.title: Convexity and relative closedness of forward sectors

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, pp. 42–45
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.1 and 7.2–7.3, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness.statement: Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness.proof:
1.1 If $x\prec y$ and $x\prec z$, splitting gives $x\sim(tx,(1-t)x)$. Consistency, positive scaling, and transitivity then give $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(ty,(1-t)z)\prec ty+(1-t)z$, so the convex combination belongs to $A_x$. [A1, algebra]

1.2 Let $y=tx+(1-t)z$ with $0<t<1$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$. Splitting gives $y\sim(ty,(1-t)y)$. If $y\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $ty$ gives $(ty,(1-t)y)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. Compose and cancel the common $(1-t)z$ by [F2], then scale by $1/t$, to get $x\prec y$. If instead $x\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $tx$ gives $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$; recombination gives $x\prec y$. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Take $y\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. If $y\in A_x$, the claim is immediate. Otherwise choose $w\in\operatorname{ri} A_x$ by [F1]. Because $\Gamma_i$ is open, choose $z=w+(1+\eta)(y-w)\in\Gamma_i$ for some $\eta>0$. For every integer $n>1+\eta$, $y_n=(1+1/n)y-z/n=w+(1-\eta/n)(y-w)$ lies in $\operatorname{ri}A_x$ by [F1], so $x\prec y_n$. Also $y=\frac{n}{n+1}y_n+\frac1{n+1}z$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(\frac n{n+1}y_n,\frac1{n+1}z)\prec y$; scaling by $(n+1)/n$ and using the reversible split of $y$ gives $(y_n,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Consistency adds the same spectator $z/n$ to $x\prec y_n$, and transitivity with step 2.1 gives $(x,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$ for every $n>1+\eta$. Apply the stability hypothesis in [A1] to bases $x,y$, fixed positive equal-mass represented spectators $z,y$, and the tail sequence $\epsilon_m=1/(m+n_0)$ with $n_0>1+\eta$. It follows that $x\prec y$. Thus every relative closure point belongs to $A_x$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

lem-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space-.title: The cost-zero offset construction is a real vector space

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B, pp. 76–79
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space-.statement: For the construction in [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]], $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling; $V_F$ is a real vector space and its displayed operations are representative-independent.
lem-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space-.proof:
1.1 The relation $\approx_0$ is reflexive because $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, and symmetric by definition. Suppose $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma'\approx_0\Gamma''$. The triangle inequality gives both directed costs between $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma''$ at most zero. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose a finite reverse witness of cost $d<\epsilon$; such witnesses exist because the reverse infimum is zero. Every forward witness of cost $c$ closes with it, so [F2] gives $c+d\ge0$, hence $c>-\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows every forward witness has nonnegative cost and its infimum is at least zero; the same argument reverses the direction. Both infima are therefore zero, proving transitivity. The same argument proves product compatibility: subadditivity makes both product costs at most zero, and any finite reverse witness bounds every forward product witness below by a quantity tending to zero. Positive homogeneity gives scaling compatibility directly. Thus $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling, and the quotient is a commutative monoid. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Reversible splitting [A1] gives accessible transitions in both directions between $(s+t)\Gamma$ and $s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. Extensivity makes each such edge have zero entropy cost. Any reverse witness bounds all forward costs below by [F2]'s closed-cycle inequality, so both infima are zero. Hence $(s+t)\Gamma\approx_0 s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. The empty type $1$ is an identity under composition; its reassociation and permutation identifications have zero cost by the type conventions. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 The pair relation $\equiv$ is reflexive using unit catalyst $1$ and symmetric by swapping the two sides. Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via catalyst $C$, and $(A',B')\equiv(A'',B'')$ via catalyst $D$. Their witnesses are
$A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C,\qquad
A'\times B''\times D\approx_0 A''\times B'\times D.$
Multiply the first equivalence by $B''\times D$, the second by $B\times C$, and compose. Reassociating and permuting gives
