$A\times B''\times(B'\times C\times D)\approx_0 A''\times B\times(B'\times C\times D),$
which witnesses $(A,B)\equiv(A'',B'')$. Hence $\equiv$ is an equivalence relation. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via $C$, so $A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C$. For an arbitrary pair $(D,E)$, multiply this witness by $D\times E$. Reassociation gives $(A\times D)\times(B'\times E)\times C\approx_0(A'\times D)\times(B\times E)\times C$, exactly the witness for $(A\times D,B\times E)\equiv(A'\times D,B'\times E)$. Apply the same argument to a change of representative of $(D,E)$ and use transitivity; addition is representative-independent. Scaling a catalyst witness by $t>0$ and using product compatibility from step 1.1 proves that positive scalar multiplication is representative-independent. Product commutativity and associativity give the additive laws, and the empty type gives $(A\times1,B\times1)=(A,B)$. Swapping a pair gives an inverse: its sum with $(A,B)$ is $(A\times B,B\times A)$, equivalent to $(1,1)$ with unit catalyst because the two product types agree up to permutation and have zero cost in both directions. Thus the classes form an abelian group with zero $[(1,1)]$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 For $t>0$, the displayed operation $t(A,B)=(tA,tB)$ satisfies $t(v+w)=tv+tw$ because scaling distributes over type composition, and $t(sv)=(ts)v$ for $s>0$ by associativity of type scaling. Also $1v=v$. The scalar-addition law for positive $s,t$ follows from step 1.2:
$(s+t)[A,B]=[(s+t)A,(s+t)B]=[sA\times tA,sB\times tB]=s[A,B]+t[A,B].$
The zero scalar is defined as the additive identity, and $(-t)v$ is defined as $t(-v)$, where $-v$ swaps the pair. [F1, step 1.2, step 3.1]

5.1 The positive scalar laws extend to negative scalars by swapping pairs. For the scalar-addition law with opposite signs, write $s-t$ with $s,t\ge0$. If $s\ge t$, positive scalar addition gives $sv=(s-t)v+tv$, so cancellation in the additive group gives $(s-t)v=sv-tv$; if $t>s$, apply the same identity to $t=(t-s)+s$ and negate. Cases with zero are immediate. For scalar composition, write each nonzero scalar as its sign times a positive magnitude; the defined action swaps the pair once for each negative sign and scales by the product of magnitudes, so $(rs)v=r(sv)$, with zero cases immediate. For distributivity over vector addition, positive scalars distribute by step 4.1 and a negative scalar distributes by taking the additive inverse of that identity. Together with the abelian-group laws in step 3.1, these are all real-vector-space axioms. [F1, step 4.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

lem-tdmath-decorated-cost-algebra.title: Algebraic properties of decorated-chain costs

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B, Eqs. 6.6–6.16, pp. 74–75
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-decorated-cost-algebra.statement: For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.
lem-tdmath-decorated-cost-algebra.proof:
1.1 A reflexive identity edge from any nonempty state of $\Gamma$ to itself has cost zero, so $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)\le0$. For a decorated closed chain, start with the compound containing every edge input $a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1}$. Apply the edge $a_0\prec b_1$ with all other edge inputs as spectators, then apply $a_1\prec b_2$ with the already produced $b_1$ and all still-unused inputs as spectators, and continue through $a_{N-1}\prec b_N$. Consistency and transitivity give $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}a_k\prec\sum_{k=1}^{N}b_k$. Since $T_N=T_0$ and the intermediate types occur once on each side, these two compounds have the same total type up to the declared reassociation and permutation. Their entropy difference is exactly the chain cost. The same-type entropy representation [F2] makes this difference nonnegative. Hence every closed-chain witness costs at least zero and $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Take finite witnesses for $(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)$ and $(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$. Run the first chain with a fixed state of $\Gamma_2$ and its second catalyst as spectators; then run the second chain with the first chain's output state and first catalyst as spectators. Consistency allows both sequences, and each fixed spectator contributes zero entropy difference. The resulting witness from $\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_2$ to $\Gamma'_1\times\Gamma'_2$ has the sum of the two costs. If both infima are finite real numbers, choose witnesses within $\epsilon/2$ of each infimum and let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. If one infimum is $-\infty$ and the other is finite, use a fixed finite witness for the latter and arbitrarily negative witnesses for the former; the product costs are unbounded below. If both are $-\infty$, choose both costs arbitrarily negative, so the product infimum is $-\infty$. If either is $+\infty$ and the other is not $-\infty$, the right side is $+\infty$ and the inequality is automatic. The mixed extended sum $+\infty+(-\infty)$ is undefined and is excluded by the Statement. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.3 A witness for $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$ is a witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ with enlarged catalyst $C_0\times C$, so $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$. Conversely, add one fixed state of the nonempty catalyst $C_0$ to every edge of an arbitrary witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Its cost is unchanged, proving the reverse inequality. Thus $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Scaling every state, type, and catalyst in a witness by $t>0$ multiplies its cost by $t$ because $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$. This gives $F(t\Gamma,t\Gamma')\le tF(\Gamma,\Gamma')$; applying the same argument with scale $1/t$ gives equality, including the extended values. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Concatenate a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ with one from $\Gamma'$ to $\Gamma''$, adding the other chain's fixed catalyst state as spectator to each edge. The result is a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma''$ whose cost is the sum. Taking finite approximations proves the triangle inequality when both costs are finite; an unbounded-below term with a finite witness in the other direction gives the corresponding $-\infty$ case; if a term is $+\infty$ and the sum is defined, the inequality is automatic. For an actual forward witness and an actual reverse witness with possibly different catalysts, add the reverse catalyst's fixed state to every forward edge and the forward catalyst's fixed state to every reverse edge. Consistency supplies these padded edges, and additivity makes each edge cost unchanged. The padded chains now have the same catalyst, so concatenate them into a closed chain; step 1.1 gives $c+d\ge0$. Thus any fixed finite reverse witness of cost $d$ bounds every forward witness below by $-d$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

lem-tdmath-reference-order.title: Ordering the two-state reference mixtures

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Lemma 2.2
Campión et al., A Survey on the Mathematical Foundations of Axiomatic Entropy, §§2–5

lem-tdmath-reference-order.statement:
Let $x_0,x_1\in X$ satisfy $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$. For every real $\lambda$, define the signed unit-mass reference map $R_\lambda:=(1-\lambda)e_{x_0}+\lambda e_{x_1}$. For all $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$,

$$R_\lambda\preceq_s R_\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\le\mu.$$

The parameters need not lie in $[0,1]$; outside that interval $R_\lambda$ is signed notation, not a compound.
lem-tdmath-reference-order.proof:
**Given:** [A1], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 Put $\delta:=\mu-\lambda$. The coefficient difference is $R_\mu-R_\lambda=\delta(e_{x_1}-e_{x_0})$ and has total zero. If $\delta>0$, its negative and positive parts are $\delta e_{x_0}$ and $\delta e_{x_1}$; if $\delta<0$, they are $(-\delta)e_{x_1}$ and $(-\delta)e_{x_0}$; if $\delta=0$, both are zero. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 If $\delta=0$, reflexivity gives $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$. If $\delta>0$, [F1] reduces this comparison to $\delta e_{x_0}\preceq\delta e_{x_1}$, which follows by positive scaling of $x_0\preceq x_1$ by $\delta$. Hence $\lambda<\mu$ implies $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $\delta<0$ and $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$, [F1] gives $(-\delta)e_{x_1}\preceq(-\delta)e_{x_0}$. Positive scaling by $1/(-\delta)$ would imply $x_1\preceq x_0$, contrary to [A1]. Thus this comparison fails when $\lambda>\mu$. The three cases prove the equivalence. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

lem-tdmath-reference-strip-coordinate.title: A unique reference coordinate inside a thermal strip

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §IV.B.1, pp. 54–56
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapter 4, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-reference-strip-coordinate.statement: Let a simple domain and its finite thermal joins satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Let $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$, and let $x$ satisfy $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$. For $0\le\lambda\le1$, write $R_\lambda$ for the compound state $((1-\lambda)x_0,\lambda x_1)$, omitting a zero coefficient at the endpoints. Then there is a unique $\lambda\in(0,1)$ with $R_\lambda\sim x$ in the common accessibility relation.
lem-tdmath-reference-strip-coordinate.proof:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3], and $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$.

1.1 For $0\le\lambda<\mu\le1$, the signed difference $R_\mu-R_\lambda=(\mu-\lambda)(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))$ has positive part $(\mu-\lambda)\iota(x_1)$ and negative part $(\mu-\lambda)\iota(x_0)$. Since $x_0\prec x_1$, positive scaling and [F2] give $R_\lambda\prec R_\mu$. A reverse comparison would, by [F2] and inverse positive scaling, give $x_1\prec x_0$, contrary to strictness. Thus the reference states are strictly ordered by parameter. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For $0<\lambda<1$, [F1] makes $(1-\lambda)x_0$ and $\lambda x_1$ thermally equivalent. By the definition of thermal equivalence, their compound is reversible with its join state. The equal-state split makes $((1-\lambda)x,\lambda x)$ reversible with its join state and with $x$. Both join states belong to the join of two scaled copies of the same simple domain, so [F3] compares them. The endpoint cases use $R_0=x_0$ and $R_1=x_1$ directly. Hence $R_\lambda$ and $x$ are comparable for every $\lambda\in[0,1]$. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Let $L=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:R_\lambda\prec x\}$. The strict endpoint comparison $x_0\prec x$ puts $0$ in $L$. Step 1.1 and transitivity make $L$ downward closed. Let $s=\sup L$. If $s>0$, then $s-1/n\in L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Since $R_{s-1/n}+(1/n)x_1=R_s+(1/n)x_0$, consistency yields $R_s+(1/n)x_0\prec x+(1/n)x_1$. Stability with bases $R_s,x$ and fixed spectators $x_0,x_1$ gives $R_s\prec x$. If $s=0$, this comparison is the given $x_0\prec x$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 If $s<1$, then $s+1/n\notin L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Step 1.2 gives comparability and the definition of $L$ excludes $R_{s+1/n}\prec x$, so $x\prec R_{s+1/n}$. The identity $R_{s+1/n}+(1/n)x_0=R_s+(1/n)x_1$ and stability yield $x\prec R_s$. If $s=1$, the strict strip gives $x\prec R_1$; together with step 2.1 this would imply $x_1\prec x$, contrary to $x\prec\prec x_1$. Thus $s<1$, and step 2.1 and the preceding stability comparison give $R_s\sim x$. [A1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 The equivalence $R_s\sim x$ also excludes $s=0$, because $R_0=x_0$ and $x_0\not\sim x$, and excludes $s=1$ by strictness of $x\prec\prec x_1$. If $R_t\sim x$ for another $t$, transitivity gives $R_s\sim R_t$; step 1.1 then forces $s=t$. Hence the parameter is unique and lies in $(0,1)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds.title: Reference entropy supremum is finite and attained

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Lemmas 2.1 and 2.3
Campión et al., A Survey on the Mathematical Foundations of Axiomatic Entropy, §§2–5

lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds.statement:
Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.
lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds.proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[F5], with $x\in X$ fixed.

1.1 Suppose no positive integer $n$ satisfies $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$. Both sides have mass $n+1$, so CH gives $ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_x\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n=1/n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$, each of mass one. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by [F2] is $R_{-n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-n\in L_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F4]

1.2 Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each positive integer $n$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>n$; [F3] gives $R_n\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $n\in L_x$. By [F2], $R_n\preceq_s e_x$ is the compound comparison $e_{x_0}+n e_{x_1}\preceq e_x+n e_{x_0}$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 For each $n$, $s-1/n$ is not an upper bound of $L_x$, so some $\lambda\in L_x$ has $\lambda>s-1/n$. Downward closure gives $s-1/n\in L_x$. Consistency then gives $R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq_s e_x+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$, because $R_{s-1/n}+n^{-1}e_{x_1}=R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_0}$. Let $K:=R_s^-$. Adding the fixed nonnegative map $K$ to both sides converts this signed comparison into the compound comparisons $R_s^++n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq e_x+K+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Their bases have equal mass because $m(R_s^+)-m(K)=1$. Stability with spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ yields $R_s^+\preceq e_x+K$, that is, $R_s\preceq_s e_x$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $s$ is an upper bound, $s+1/n\notin L_x$. CH therefore gives $e_x\preceq_s R_{s+1/n}$. Add $n^{-1}e_{x_0}$ to both sides and use $R_{s+1/n}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}=R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Adding $K=R_s^-$ converts the result to equal-mass compounds $e_x+K+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq R_s^++n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Stability with the same positive unit-mass spectators yields $e_x+K\preceq R_s^+$, or $e_x\preceq_sR_s$. Together with step 3.1 this proves $R_s\sim_s e_x$ and the claimed attainment. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

lem-tdmath-sector-interior.title: Every forward sector has nonempty interior

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 3.2, pp. 43–45
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.1 and 7.2–7.3, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-sector-interior.statement: Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.
lem-tdmath-sector-interior.proof:
1.1 Suppose $A_x$ has empty ambient interior. If $d=1$, S1 supplies a strict successor $y\ne x$; convexity puts the nondegenerate interval between $x$ and $y$ in $A_x$, contradicting empty interior. Thus take $d\ge2$. The affine hull of $A_x$ has dimension at most $d-1$. If its dimension were at most $d-2$, [F2] would give two distinct supporting hyperplanes at $x$, contradicting S2. Hence its affine hull is a hyperplane $H$; this $H$ supports $A_x$ at every point, including $x$. [A1, F2]

1.2 By S1 choose $y$ with $x\prec\prec y$. Then $y\in A_x$ and $x\notin A_y$. Transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x\subseteq H$. If $A_y$ had affine dimension at most $d-2$, [F2] would again give multiple ambient supports at $y$, contrary to S2. Thus $\operatorname{aff}A_y=H$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.3 Choose $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H A_y$ by [F3]. The segment from $w$ to $x$ is contained in $H\cap\Gamma_i$ by convexity of both sets, starts in $A_y$, and ends outside $A_y$. Its intersection with $A_y$ is closed by relative closedness [F1], so it has a last point $z$ before $x$. Points immediately after $z$ on this segment lie outside $A_y$ and, because $A_y$ is closed in the open set $\Gamma_i$, outside $\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. Thus $z\in\partial_H\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. The support statement [F2] supplies a nonzero functional on $H$ whose zero hyperplane supports $A_y$ at $z$. [F1, F2, F3, choose]

2.1 Extend this functional to the ambient Euclidean space by taking its normal vector in the direction space of $H$. Its zero hyperplane contains the within-$H$ support and is not $H$ itself. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y$, so the extended plane supports $A_z$ at $z$; the plane $H$ also supports $A_z$. These are distinct, contradicting S2 at $z$. Therefore $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior. [A1, F1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation.title: Spectator cancellation and signed-order algebra

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 2.1 and §II.D

lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation.statement: Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.
lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation.proof:
**Given:** [F1], [A1], and [F2].

1.1 For equal-total $u,v$, $d=v-u$ has finite support and total sum zero. Pointwise $d=d^+-d^-$, so finite-sum linearity gives $m(d^+)-m(d^-)=0$; both maps are finite-support and nonnegative. Thus the definition in [F2] compares equal-mass compounds. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, set $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$; then $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. [F1, F2]

1.2 Suppose $A+C\preceq B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each positive integer $n$, pointwise addition gives $A=n(A/n)$ and $B=n(B/n)$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\preceq B/n+C/n$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/n$ one at a time by $B/n$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/n$ as spectators; after all replacements, $A+C/n\preceq B+C/n$. Apply stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ to obtain $A\preceq B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\preceq B$ gives $A+C\preceq B+C$ by consistency. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For nonnegative $u,v$, step 1.1 gives $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. Cancellation from step 1.2 shows $u\preceq v$ exactly when $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$, which is $u\preceq_s v$. For general signed maps, adding a common map leaves $v-u$ unchanged, so it leaves signed comparison unchanged. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, then consistency combines $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-\preceq(w-v)^+$ into a comparison between the sums of their negative and positive parts. The two sums have a common pointwise minimum; cancel it by step 1.2. The remaining maps are precisely $(w-u)^-$ and $(w-u)^+$, so $u\preceq_s w$. The same sum-and-cancel argument applied to two independent signed comparisons proves closure under their addition; reflexivity follows from $0\preceq0$. [A1, F2, step 1.2] ∎

lem-tdmath-thermal-class-dichotomy.title: Thermal classes either fill the domain or split an adiabat

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 4.6, pp. 56–57
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapter 4, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-thermal-class-dichotomy.statement: Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a simple domain satisfying the forward-sector hypotheses and T1–T4. Let $S$ be the additive extensive entropy supplied by [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] after CH for its finite scaled products is proved by [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]. Then either all pairs of states in $\Gamma$ are thermally equivalent, or there are $x,y$ on one entropy level (equivalently, one adiabat $\partial A_x$ by [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]) with $x\not\sim_T y$.
lem-tdmath-thermal-class-dichotomy.proof:
1.1 Use [F7]'s common mathematical energy orientation for the proof coordinates. Apply [F2] using [F1] after dividing represented coefficient maps by the fixed positive type weight $w_\Gamma$, as specified in [A1]. Multiply the resulting unit-state entropy by $w_\Gamma$ to evaluate represented states; this positive factor preserves all same-type order comparisons. Write $S(x)$ for that represented-state value. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] and additivity imply concavity: for $0<t<1$, accessibility of $(tx,(1-t)y)$ to $tx+(1-t)y$ gives $tS(x)+(1-t)S(y)\le S(tx+(1-t)y)$. By [F3], $S$ is strictly increasing in energy at fixed work coordinate. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F7]

1.2 Fix a work coordinate $v$ and let $J_v:=\{u:(u,v)\in\Gamma\}$, an open interval. The restriction $s_v(u)=S(u,v)$ is finite, concave, continuous by [F4], and strictly increasing by [F3]. For an interior $u$, concavity makes the right secant slopes nonincreasing as the secant endpoint moves right, and the left secant slopes monotone as the endpoint approaches $u$; hence the one-sided derivative limits $s'_{v,+}(u)$ and $s'_{v,-}(u)$ exist. Choose $a<u<b$ in $J_v$: the secants to $a,b$ bound those limits, so they are finite, and concavity gives $s'_-\ge s'_+$. Monotonicity gives nonnegative slopes. If $s'_+(u)=0$, then for every $z>u$ concavity bounds $(s_v(z)-s_v(u))/(z-u)\le s'_+(u)=0$, contradicting strict increase. Thus $s'_-\ge s'_+>0$. Define $\Theta(u,v)=[1/s'_{v,-}(u),1/s'_{v,+}(u)]$, a nonempty compact interval of positive finite reciprocal slopes. [A1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 Suppose the second alternative fails, so each adiabat contains one thermal-equivalence class. By [F1]–[F2], $A_x=\{y:S(y)\ge S(x)\}$. Continuity of $S$ and strict increase in energy at fixed work coordinate imply that every point with $S=\sigma$ has arbitrarily nearby points with larger and smaller entropy; hence each entropy level $E_\sigma=\{x:S(x)=\sigma\}$ is a forward-sector boundary. The supposition makes each $E_\sigma$ lie in one thermal class. Let $R=S(\Gamma)$ and, for each thermal class $C_\alpha$, put $R_\alpha=\{S(x):x\in C_\alpha\}$. These sets partition $R$: two distinct classes cannot share a level under the supposition. The range $R$ is an interval, since any two points of the convex domain are joined by a segment and the continuous entropy takes every intermediate value along it. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6]

2.1 Fix $x=(u_1,v_1)$ and $y=(u_2,v_2)$ of this same simple type, and let $U=u_1+u_2$. The admissible energy splits form the open interval $D=\{w:(U-w,v_1)\in\Gamma,\ (w,v_2)\in\Gamma\}$, which contains $u_2$. Define $g(w)=s_{v_1}(U-w)+s_{v_2}(w)$. For the join state $J(x,y)$, T2 gives an admissible split $q$ whose pair is reversible with the join. For every other split $p$, T1 gives $p\prec J(x,y)\prec q$, so $p\prec q$. The pair states $p,q$ are finite compounds of two copies of this same simple type; [F1]–[F2] and their entropy representation therefore give $g(p)\le g(q)$. Thus $q$ maximizes $g$. If the initial split $x,y$ is reversible with the join, it is equivalent to $q$; entropy representation gives equal entropy, so it too maximizes $g$. Conversely, if $u_2$ maximizes $g$, then $g(u_2)=g(q)$, and [F1]–[F2] make the initial pair reversible with $q$; composing with $q\sim J(x,y)$ shows $x\sim_T y$. For a concave function at an interior point, maximality is equivalent to $g'_+(u_2)\le0\le g'_-(u_2)$: right secants are bounded above by the right derivative and left secants below by the left derivative. Here
$g'_+(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,+}(u_2),\qquad
g'_-(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,-}(u_2).$
The two inequalities are exactly $s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)\le s'_{v_2,-}(u_2)$ and $s'_{v_2,+}(u_2)\le s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)$, which say the positive slope intervals intersect; reciprocal reverses their endpoints, so this is equivalent to $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(y)\ne\varnothing$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.2]

3.1 Let $T_\alpha$ be one thermal class. The compact intervals $\Theta(x)$, $x\in T_\alpha$, pairwise intersect by step 2.1. For any finite subfamily, pairwise intersection implies common intersection: the largest left endpoint is no greater than the smallest right endpoint, since the intervals attaining those two endpoints intersect. Fix $x_0\in T_\alpha$; the sets $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(x_0)$ are closed subsets of the compact interval $\Theta(x_0)$ and have the finite-intersection property. Compactness [F5] gives a common point, so $I_\alpha:=\bigcap_{x\in T_\alpha}\Theta(x)$ is a nonempty compact interval. If distinct classes had intersecting common intervals, representatives $x,y$ would have intersecting $\Theta$ intervals and would be thermally equivalent by step 2.1, a contradiction. Thus the intervals $I_\alpha$ for distinct classes are disjoint and strictly ordered on the real line; use this as the order of the classes. [A2, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 For each work coordinate $v$, strict continuity of $s_v$ maps the open interval $J_v$ onto an open interval $R_v\subset R$. On $R_v$, the level-to-class map is nondecreasing: as $u$ increases, concavity makes both one-sided slopes nonincreasing, so both endpoints of $\Theta(u,v)$ are nondecreasing. If two such intervals $\Theta$ are disjoint, monotonicity of both endpoints forces the earlier interval to lie strictly below the later one; by step 3.1, this is the class order. The local class maps agree on overlaps of $R_v$ because each entropy level lies in one class. The open intervals $R_v$ cover $R$. Any compact subinterval of $R$ has a finite subcover by these intervals by [F5]; its intersection graph is connected, since otherwise the connected subinterval would be split into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Chaining the local orders through overlaps proves that the class map is nondecreasing on all of $R$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 3.1]

5.1 Fix $\sigma\in R_\alpha$ and $x\in E_\sigma$. T4 gives $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$. Entropy representation gives $S(x_0)<\sigma<S(x_1)$, and their levels belong to the same class $R_\alpha$. The global nondecreasing order from step 4.1 forces every level between them, including an open neighborhood of $\sigma$, into $R_\alpha$. Thus each class set is open in the interval $R$. Since these disjoint open sets partition connected $R$, only one nonempty class exists. Under the supposition, all states are thermally equivalent, proving the dichotomy. [A2, F2, step 4.1] ∎

lem-tdmath-thermal-scaling-invariance.title: Scaling invariance of thermal equivalence

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 4.1, p. 51
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapter 4, complete 607-page edition

lem-tdmath-thermal-scaling-invariance.statement: Under T1–T3 and the equal-state reversible split in [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]], if $x\sim_T y$ then $s x\sim_T t y$ for every $s,t>0$.
lem-tdmath-thermal-scaling-invariance.proof:
1.1 Let $x$ be any typed state and $s>0$. The state $z=(1+s)x$ in the scaled type has the equal-state reversible split with fractions $1/(1+s)$ and $s/(1+s)$; its two components are exactly $x$ and $sx$. Thus $(x,sx)$ is reversible with its join, which by definition is $x\sim_T sx$. The same argument gives $y\sim_T ty$. [A1, given]

2.1 Since $x\sim_T y$, symmetry gives $y\sim_T x$. Transitivity with $x\sim_T sx$ yields $y\sim_T sx$; symmetry then gives $sx\sim_T y$. Transitivity with $y\sim_T ty$ now yields $sx\sim_T ty$. [A1, step 1.1, given] ∎

pthm-td-contact-product-comparison.title: Conditional contact calibrator and product comparison

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 4.8 and §§IV.A–IV.C
André Thess, The Lieb–Yngvason Machine: A didactical tool for the definition of entropy in classical thermodynamics, §§2–4
Goddard, The second law of thermodynamics as variation on a theme of Carathéodory, §§2–3

pthm-td-contact-product-comparison.statement:
For every declared finite family of simple-system domains closed under the thermal joins of [[def-td-thermal-join]], assume the accessibility axioms A1–A6, the simple-system assumptions A7 and S1–S3, the contact assumptions T1–T4, the universal thermal-equilibrium range T5, and equilibrium-join coherence C1, with the exact formulations in [[post-td-accessibility-a1-a6]], [[post-td-simple-system-geometric-axioms]], [[post-td-thermal-join-axioms]], [[post-td-universal-thermal-range]], and [[post-td-equilibrium-join-coherence]]. Then for any two simple types $i,j$, there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $i$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $j$ such that

$$ (x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0). $$

Moreover, for this fixed pair $i,j$, every finite separated product made only from positive scaled copies of $i$ and $j$ satisfies the comparison hypothesis: any two equal-formal-mass states $A,B$ of that product type satisfy $A\prec B$ or $B\prec A$. No comparison conclusion for products involving a third primitive type is contained in this pairwise result. These are conditional model deductions. In particular, the conclusion is not claimed from the printed Theorem 4.8 interface with T1–T4 alone; the local mathematical supplier explicitly requires the additional T5 and C1 branch.
pthm-td-contact-product-comparison.proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[A5] and the exact mathematical statements [F1]–[F2].

1.1 Fix two simple types $i,j$ in the declared family. Give every primitive material its unit amount vector and use the aggregate composition of [[def-td-scaled-products-and-comparison]] for each scaled, separated or joined type $\Gamma$; its sum is $w_\Gamma>0$ unless the type is empty. Construct [F2]'s encoded state and interpretation maps using the physical tagged scaling maps: a raw coefficient $a>0$ at $(\Gamma,x)$ denotes the preparation $(a/w_\Gamma)x$. The map preserves aggregate composition and formal mass, and distinct raw tags remain distinct. The interpretations of $\iota_{s\Gamma}(\delta_s x)$ and $s\iota_\Gamma(x)$ are the same declared scaled preparation by composition of scaling maps; reflexivity gives reversible transport. When factor coefficients combine or split, [A1]'s reversible-splitting axiom supplies reversibility, so the pullback inherits composition, positive scaling and stability from [A1]. Dividing fixed-type encoded maps by $w_\Gamma$ and scaling back preserves and reflects comparisons, so the one-copy forward sectors and all geometry in [A2] are unchanged. Any common sign chosen in the mathematical orientation deduction is used only for proof coordinates $u'=\varepsilon U$; the physical energy $U$ retains its fixed SI meaning, units and all independently adopted positive-$S_U$ or calibration qualifications. Since the same sign is applied to each component and join proof coordinate, summed-energy identities are preserved. Thus the actual preparation model supplies the exact formal conventions and all order/geometric hypotheses required by [F1]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 By [A3], the physical operation [[def-td-thermal-join]] supplies T1–T4 with the same summed-energy coordinates and reversible splitting used in [F1]. Its pair and join retain the same aggregate composition by [[def-td-thermal-join]], so their encoded weights both equal $w_i+w_j$; no mass-one join is compared to an unweighted mass-two pair. [A3, F1, given]

2.1 [A4] supplies the separately stated T5 quantifiers for every ordered simple-system pair, and [A5] supplies the separate C1 nested-join equivalence. Thus every premise of [F1], including its two stronger contact inputs, is met on the whole declared join-closed family. [A4, A5, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Apply [F1] to this pair $i,j$. Its first conclusion is states $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ with $(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0)$; its second is comparison for every finite separated product made from scaled copies of these two types. This is precisely the stated pairwise conclusion. [F1, step 2.1] ∎
pthm-td-contact-product-comparison.physical_scope: Conditional consequence of the adopted A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5 and C1 assumptions for the declared finite thermal-contact family; not an unconditional law for real materials.

pthm-td-entropy-under-product-comparison.title: Entropy representation for finite separated products

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorems 2.2 and 4.8 and §IV.B
André Thess, The Lieb–Yngvason Machine: A didactical tool for the definition of entropy in classical thermodynamics, §§2–4
Goddard, The second law of thermodynamics as variation on a theme of Carathéodory, §§2–3

pthm-td-entropy-under-product-comparison.statement:
Let $I$ be a nonempty, possibly infinite set of primitive system labels. Assume the declared family includes every finite separated product and every finite thermal join, and that every finite join-closed subfamily satisfies the hypotheses of [[pthm-td-contact-product-comparison]]. Also assume the explicit finite-factor representation of [[def-td-scaled-products-and-comparison]] and the Axiom of Choice. Then there is a single dimensionless function $\widetilde S$ on all states of the declared finite-factor family that is additive under separation, extensive under every admitted positive scaling, and characterizes every equal-composition comparison:

$$ A\prec B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \widetilde S(A)\le \widetilde S(B). $$

For each simple chart, A7 also makes $\widetilde S$ concave on every convex region where the stated recombination operation is admitted. The result does not set the entropy unit to $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, determine additive constants across different reaction compositions, or establish empirical validity of the contact assumptions.
pthm-td-entropy-under-product-comparison.proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[A5].

1.1 Fix a finite set of primitive labels from $I$. For every pair in this set, [A2] supplies a strict calibrator and comparison hypothesis on all finite products formed from that pair; the relation also satisfies the six accessibility assumptions of the physical model. These are the pairwise contact inputs required by [A3], not a claim that the pair theorem alone compares products involving three or more primitive types. The factors have the explicit tagged finite representation in [A5]. [A2, A5, given]

2.1 Since $I$ is nonempty, choose a primitive type $m$ as the distinguished meter label. Applying [A2] to the ordered pair $(m,m)$ supplies a strict meter pair $z_0\prec\prec z_1$ in $\Gamma_m$. For each $j\ne m$, applying [A2] to the ordered pair $(j,m)$ supplies states $a_j,b_j\in\Gamma_j$ and $c_j,d_j\in\Gamma_m$ with $a_j\prec\prec b_j$, $c_j\prec\prec d_j$, and $(a_j,d_j)\sim(b_j,c_j)$, exactly the calibrator orientation required by [A3]. Choice [A1] selects the reference states, same-type entropy representatives and calibrator data simultaneously across $I$, exactly as [A3] requires. Use the composition-preserving coefficient-map interpretation constructed in [A2]: each actual state is represented by its type-weighted point mass, and scalar amount $t$ has the encoded state value $t$ times that state entropy. In [A3], same-type unit-label representations are converted back to represented-state values by their positive type weights, so the calibration describes the original tagged preparations, not independently rescaled entropy units for joined types. Each compound contains only finitely many tagged factors. The empty unit has value zero as the empty entropy sum; every nonempty compound is a finite sum of tagged factor entropies. Applying [A3] gives a single function $\widetilde S$ on the family of all such finite compounds, additive on concatenation, homogeneous under each positive scale, and order-equivalent to $\prec$ for each equal-composition comparison. No infinite sum is introduced because every state has finite support. [A1, A2, A3, A5, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Let $x,y$ lie in one simple chart and $0<t<1$. By [A4], the scaled pair $(t x,(1-t)y)$ compares to the recombined state $t x+(1-t)y$. The representation in step 2.1 turns that comparison into $$ t\widetilde S(x)+(1-t)\widetilde S(y)\le \widetilde S(t x+(1-t)y), $$ where additivity and extensivity evaluate the pair entropy. This is precisely concavity on the admitted convex chart; the endpoint weights $t=0,1$ give equality. [A3, A4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
pthm-td-entropy-under-product-comparison.physical_scope: An order representation for the declared finite family of simple systems under the adopted contact assumptions; the entropy is dimensionless until an independent physical calibration fixes its unit.

pthm-td-universal-mixing-entropy.title: Conditional weak entropy principle across mixing channels

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 6.1 and §VI.B

pthm-td-universal-mixing-entropy.statement:
Let $\mathcal G\ne\varnothing$ be a finite-factor-closed network of [[def-td-cross-type-reaction-network]]. Assume the contact hypotheses of [[pthm-td-entropy-under-product-comparison]] provide a finite real baseline entropy $\sigma_\Gamma$ on each type. Also assume that network satisfies A1–A6, its exact decorated-chain cost $F$ has the no-sinks property defined there, and the Axiom of Choice. Then there is a real offset $B(\Gamma)$ for each type, additive under finite composition and extensive under every positive scaling, such that the corrected entropy

$$S_\Gamma(x):=\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)$$

is nondecreasing across every admitted channel transition: if $(\Gamma,x)\mathcal R(\Gamma',y)$, then $S_\Gamma(x)\le S_{\Gamma'}(y)$. The conclusion is weak monotonicity only. It does not assert a no-gap identity, uniqueness of $B$, strict increase, or a global entropy principle for networks that fail the stated hypotheses.
pthm-td-universal-mixing-entropy.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F4].

1.1 Fix an admitted transition $(\Gamma,x)\mathcal R(\Gamma',y)$. [F1] supplies finite baseline state values on both endpoint types, and [F2] identifies the decorated-chain cost convention used for this pair. Use the composition-preserving type-weighted representation from [F1]'s construction: interpret each encoded coefficient by its amount divided by the positive type weight, keeping the raw scaled and joined tags distinct. The network compares equal formal masses, and this interpretation preserves its admitted endpoint relation and each finite baseline entropy sum; hence each physical finite-chain witness and its coefficient-map image have the same real edge costs. Reversible regrouping of factors uses the adopted reversible-splitting axiom in [F2], so it changes neither the represented endpoints nor their baseline values. The cost $F$ used by [F3] is therefore this exact witness infimum, not one inferred from coordinate equality. Applying [F3] to this exact transition gives $$ \sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma'). $$ If the edge exists, the one-edge chain makes $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty$, so this inequality has an ordinary real right side under the stated no-sinks hypothesis. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 The network’s no-sinks condition and [A1] match the hypotheses of [F4]; its cost is the same $F$ as in step 1.1 by [F2] and [F3]. Thus [F4] supplies one offset function $B$, common to all types, with additivity, positive-scale extensivity and $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ for every pair. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Subtract the bound in step 2.1 from that in step 1.1: $$ [\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)+B(\Gamma')]-[\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)]\ge0. $$ By the definition of $S$ in the Statement, this is $S_{\Gamma'}(y)\ge S_\Gamma(x)$. The same $B$ works for every admitted transition, proving the conditional weak entropy principle. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
pthm-td-universal-mixing-entropy.physical_scope: Conditional entropy monotonicity across the declared cross-type mixing and reaction network; no-gap, uniqueness, strict increase, and empirical universality are not asserted.

rem-td-entropy-construction-hypotheses.title: Scope of the accessibility entropy construction

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.D–II.F, IV.B–IV.C and VI
André Thess, The Lieb–Yngvason Machine: A didactical tool for the definition of entropy in classical thermodynamics, §§2–4
Goddard, The second law of thermodynamics as variation on a theme of Carathéodory, §§2–3
Samuel J. Ling, William Moebs, and Jeff Sanny, University Physics Volume 2, §4.1 Reversible and Irreversible Processes
Samuel J. Ling, William Moebs, and Jeff Sanny, University Physics Volume 2, §4.4 Statements of the Second Law of Thermodynamics
Samuel J. Ling, William Moebs, and Jeff Sanny, University Physics Volume 2, §4.6 Entropy

rem-td-entropy-construction-hypotheses.physical_scope: Interpretation and limitations of the conditional accessibility, product and mixing entropy results on this page.

thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representati.title: Additive extensive representation of compound comparison

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 2.2
Campión et al., A Survey on the Mathematical Foundations of Axiomatic Entropy, §§2–5

thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representati.statement:
Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.
thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representati.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F4].

1.1 In the strict-reference case, [F3] gives $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_{x_0}$ exactly for $\lambda\le0$, and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_{x_1}$ exactly for $\lambda\le1$. Their suprema are therefore $S(x_0)=0$ and $S(x_1)=1$. [F2, F3]

1.2 Let $C=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ have mass $M$ and set $q_C:=\sum_i a_iS(x_i)$. Discard any zero terms in this presentation using [F4]. If the support is empty, $C=0$, $M=q_C=0$ and $C_R=0$, so signed reflexivity gives the claimed equivalence. Otherwise each remaining coefficient is strictly positive. For each remaining constituent, [F2] gives $e_{x_i}\sim_sR_{S(x_i)}$; positive scaling and finite repeated use of composition combine these into $C\sim_s C_R$, where $C_R:=\sum_i a_iR_{S(x_i)}=(M-q_C)e_{x_0}+q_Ce_{x_1}$. This calculation is valid for signed coefficients because the signed relation is additive and translation-invariant by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.2 to both $A$ and $B$, and write $q_A,q_B$ for the resulting scalar sums. Since $A\sim_sA_R$ and $B\sim_sB_R$, transitivity gives $A\preceq B$ exactly when $A_R\preceq_sB_R$. Their masses agree, and $B_R-A_R=(q_B-q_A)(e_{x_1}-e_{x_0})$; [F3] therefore gives $A_R\preceq_sB_R$ exactly when $q_A\le q_B$. This proves the representation formula. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.2]

3.1 In the no-strict-pair case, take any $x,y\in X$. By [F4] their unit compounds have equal mass one, so CH gives one of $x\preceq y$ or $y\preceq x$; if exactly one held it would be a strict pair, so both hold. Fix $r\in X$. Let $C$ have mass $M$. If $M=0$, [F4] gives $C=0$, and reflexivity handles this empty compound without applying the positive-scaling axiom at zero. If $M>0$, use the canonical finite decomposition over the support from [F4]; every coefficient there is positive. Scale each constituent equivalence $e_x\sim e_r$ by its positive coefficient and compose the finitely many comparisons to obtain $C\sim M e_r$. Thus equal-mass $A,B$ are both empty when their common mass is zero, and otherwise each is equivalent to the same $M e_r$; hence they are equivalent in both cases. For a constant $S(x)=c$, both compound values equal $cM$, including zero for empty compounds, so the representation equivalence holds. [A1, F1, F4, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-affine-entropy-uniqueness.title: Uniqueness up to a positive affine transformation

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 2.3
Campión et al., A Survey on the Mathematical Foundations of Axiomatic Entropy, §§2–5

thm-tdmath-affine-entropy-uniqueness.statement: Assume the strict-reference hypotheses and let $S$ be the normalized representation from [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]. Let $T:X\to\mathbb R$ be another additive extensive representation of the same comparisons: for every finite compound $C=\sum_i c_i e_{x_i}$ define $T(C):=\sum_i c_iT(x_i)$, and require $C\preceq D$ iff $T(C)\le T(D)$ whenever $m(C)=m(D)$. Then there are unique $a>0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that $T(x)=aS(x)+b$ for every $x\in X$. Conversely every such positive affine change represents the same comparisons.
thm-tdmath-affine-entropy-uniqueness.proof:
**Given:** [F1], [F2], and [A1].

1.1 Fix $x\in X$ and put $s=S(x)$. The equivalence $x\sim_sR_s$ in [F1] says that the positive and negative parts of their coefficient difference compare in both directions. Since $T$ represents the same order, their finite $T$-sums are equal. By its definition on finite compounds and linearity of finite sums, the signed value of $R_s$ is $(1-s)T(x_0)+sT(x_1)$, including when $s\notin[0,1]$. Thus $T(x)=T(x_0)+[T(x_1)-T(x_0)]S(x)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Because $x_0\preceq x_1$ but not conversely, the exact representation property of $T$ gives $T(x_0)<T(x_1)$. Hence $a:=T(x_1)-T(x_0)>0$ and $b:=T(x_0)$ give the asserted form. Conversely, multiplying both sides of any represented-value inequality by $a>0$ and adding the same $b$ times the common compound mass preserves and reflects its order; therefore $aS+b$ represents the same comparisons. The parameters are unique by evaluating at $x_0$ and $x_1$, where $S$ equals $0$ and $1$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration.title: Calibration of an arbitrary family of simple-system entropies

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 2.5 and §IV.B.2, pp. 27–29, 56–59
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration.statement:
Let $I$ be a nonempty set of primitive simple-system labels containing a distinguished meter label $m$. Assume every finite separated product is explicitly represented by its finitely many tagged elementary factors; positive scaling and finite product are the only identifications. Suppose the join-closed family satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]], and fix a strict meter pair $z_0\prec\prec z_1$ in $\Gamma_m$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Then one can choose, for every $i\in I$, an additive constant and positive scale for its same-type entropy so that

$$S\big((t_1i_1,x_1),\ldots,(t_ni_n,x_n)\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^n t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$$

is additive, extensive, and characterizes every same-composition comparison on every finite separated product. No conclusion is asserted for transitions that change composition.
thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration.proof:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Use the positive type normalization in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] whenever invoking [F2]; state entropies evaluate represented maps $\iota(x)$, and their unit-label entropy density is $S_i(x)/w_{\Gamma_i}$. Apply [F2] to the meter type and choose its entropy $S_m$ so $S_m(z_0)=0$ and $S_m(z_1)=1$. Set the meter reference to $r_m=z_0$, and use [A1] to choose a reference state $r_i$ and one same-type entropy representative for every $i\ne m$. For each $i\ne m$, use [F1] to choose calibrator states $a_i,b_i\in\Gamma_i$ and $c_i,d_i\in\Gamma_m$ such that $a_i\prec\prec b_i$, $c_i\prec\prec d_i$, and $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$; also choose $r_i\in\Gamma_i$. For the meter label set $a_m=c_m=z_0$ and $b_m=d_m=z_1$; the two pairs $(z_0,z_1)$ and $(z_1,z_0)$ are the same two-copy meter compound up to permutation. Write $S_i^0$ for the selected entropy representative, with $S_m^0=S_m$, and put $\Delta_i=S_i^0(b_i)-S_i^0(a_i)>0$ and $\mu_i=S_m(d_i)-S_m(c_i)>0$. Define $S_i(x):=\frac{\mu_i}{\Delta_i}\bigl(S_i^0(x)-S_i^0(r_i)\bigr)$. Then $S_i(r_i)=0$ and $S_i(b_i)-S_i(a_i)=\mu_i$, matching the meter entropy increment across the chosen calibrator endpoints. For $i=m$, $\Delta_m=\mu_m=1$, so this agrees with the fixed meter normalization. [A1, F1, F2, choose]

2.1 For a finite separated compound $A$ with factors $(t_\ell i_\ell,x_\ell)$, define $S(A):=\sum_\ell t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$. The sum is finite and invariant under reordering; concatenating compounds adds the sums, and scaling every amount by $t>0$ multiplies it by $t$. The explicit-factor convention in the Statement therefore makes $S$ well-defined, additive, and extensive. [A1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Fix a composition with amounts $M_i$ for finitely many labels and let $A,B$ be two states of that same composition. For a state $x$ of type $i$, put
$s_i(x):=\frac{S_i(x)-S_i(a_i)}{\mu_i}.$
The same-type entropy representation and the CH for type $i$ show
$\iota(x)\sim_s(1-s_i(x))\iota(a_i)+s_i(x)\iota(b_i).$
Indeed, the signed difference has total coefficient zero and $S_i$-value zero, so its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy and therefore compare both ways by [F2]. The calibrator relation gives
$(\iota(b_i)-\iota(a_i))\sim_s(\iota(d_i)-\iota(c_i))$
by taking the signed difference of $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$ and canceling common terms with [F3]. Add and scale these identities over the finitely many factors of $A$. With
$q_i(A):=\sum_{\ell:\,i_\ell=i}t_\ell s_i(x_\ell),$
the resulting signed map is
$A\sim_s \sum_i M_i \iota(a_i)+\sum_i q_i(A)(\iota(d_i)-\iota(c_i)),$
where the sums range over the finite support of the composition. The same holds for $B$. Since they have the same composition, the reference base cancels, and $B-A$ is signed-equivalent to the finite meter map
$D:=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)(\iota(d_i)-\iota(c_i)).$
Extend the meter entropy linearly to raw finite signed coefficient maps using density $S_m(z)/w_{\Gamma_m}$ at a meter raw tag $(\Gamma_m,z)$; in particular its value on $\iota(z)$ is $S_m(z)$. Then
$S_m(D)=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)\mu_i=S(B)-S(A).$
The positive and negative parts of $D$ have equal mass. If $S(A)\le S(B)$, the same-type entropy representation [F2] for finite meter products gives $D^-\prec D^+$, hence $D$ compares in the forward signed direction. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F3] transfer this to $A\prec B$. Conversely, if $A\prec B$, the same signed equivalences and translation in [F3] give $D^-\prec D^+$. The meter representation in [F2] then forces $S_m(D)=S(B)-S(A)\ge0$. Reversing the entropy inequality gives the reverse comparison. Thus $S$ characterizes every same-composition comparison. Each particular comparison uses only finitely many labels; no infinite sum or uncountable product occurs. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The meter normalization fixes the multiplicative unit. Changing the chosen reference state for type $i$ changes only its additive constant; on a finite compound these constants contribute amount-weighted conserved-type offsets. This proves the stated freedom and completes the construction. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrato.title: Contact calibrators under explicit join coherence

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorems 4.5–4.8, pp. 55–59
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrato.statement:
Let $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ be simple domains in a family of finite thermal joins satisfying A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5, and C1 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $\Gamma_2$ such that

$$(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0).$$

Moreover, for every fixed finite composition of scaled copies of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, any two equal-mass states of that same composition are comparable (CH). The conclusion is conditional on the explicitly stated join-coherence and universal-range assumptions C1 and T5.
thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrato.proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[A2], [F1]–[F5], and [F8].

1.1 Work in [F8]'s common affine mathematical energy orientation, without redefining any physical energy or calibration. Apply [F1] and [F2] to each simple type, including every finite join, using the positive normalization by its fixed weight in [A1]. Throughout, entropy at a state means its represented-state value: $w_\Gamma$ times its unit-point-mass representation. This normalization preserves order and finite scalar amounts. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] makes each resulting entropy concave, since the comparison of a scaled pair with its convex-combination state translates under the representation to the concavity inequality. By [F4], each entropy is strictly increasing with energy at fixed work coordinates. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F8]

1.2 Use T5 to choose $\bar x\in\Gamma_1$ and $\bar y\in\Gamma_2$ with $\bar x\sim_T\bar y$. Let $\phi=J_{12}(\bar x,\bar y)$ and consider its adiabat $\partial A_\phi$. T2 gives every $Z$ on that adiabat at least one split $Z=J_{12}(x_Z,y_Z)$ with $x_Z\sim_T y_Z$. [A2, F4, choose]

2.1 Suppose a join state $Z$ on $\partial A_\phi$ has two distinct equilibrium splits $(x^{(1)},y^{(1)})$ and $(x^{(2)},y^{(2)})$. By the definition of $\sim_T$, both pairs are reversible with $Z$, hence mutually accessible compounds. Their work coordinates are fixed by $Z$ and their total energies equal its energy. If the first-component energies agreed, both component states in the splits would agree, so distinctness forces unequal first-component energies. If $u_{x^{(1)}}<u_{x^{(2)}}$, fixed-work comparison [F4] gives $x^{(1)}\prec\prec x^{(2)}$; conservation of total energy gives $u_{y^{(2)}}<u_{y^{(1)}}$, hence $y^{(2)}\prec\prec y^{(1)}$. Taking $(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)=(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},y^{(2)},y^{(1)})$ gives $(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0)$ because both split compounds are reversible with $Z$. If the first energies occur in the opposite order, swap the two splits and obtain the same calibrator form. Therefore, if no calibrator exists, every $Z\in\partial A_\phi$ has a unique equilibrium split. [A2, F4, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 Assume no calibrator exists. For any equilibrium split $(x_Z,y_Z)$ of $Z\in\partial A_\phi$, reversibility with $Z$ and the common adiabat give $(x_Z,y_Z)\sim(\bar x,\bar y)$ as compounds. By [F1], $x_Z$ and $\bar x$ are comparable; [F4] says their sectors coincide exactly when they are equivalent. If $x_Z\prec\prec\bar x$, pair reversibility gives $(\bar x,\bar y)\prec(x_Z,y_Z)$. Consistency adds $\bar y$ to $x_Z\prec\bar x$, and cancellation [F5] gives $\bar y\prec y_Z$. If $y_Z\prec\bar y$, consistency and the pair comparison instead cancel to give $\bar x\prec x_Z$, a contradiction. Thus $\bar y\prec\prec y_Z$, making a calibrator. The case $\bar x\prec\prec x_Z$ is symmetric: it gives $y_Z\prec\prec\bar y$, again a calibrator. Since neither is allowed under the assumption, $x_Z\sim\bar x$. Adding spectators to the two directions and cancelling by [F5] then gives both $\bar y\prec y_Z$ and $y_Z\prec\bar y$, so $y_Z\sim\bar y$. Thus every split on this adiabat has components in the corresponding component adiabats. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Under the no-calibrator assumption, fix a first-component work coordinate $v_1$ in the projection of $\partial A_{\bar x}$. The boundary-graph result [F4] gives exactly one state $x_*$ on that component adiabat at $v_1$. Every split of a join state on $\partial A_\phi$ with first work coordinate $v_1$ therefore has first component $x_*$. Each split is thermal, so $x_*\sim_T y_Z$ for its second component. T3 makes all such $y_Z$ thermally equivalent, and C1 makes each joined state $J(x_*,y_Z)=Z$ thermally equivalent to $x_*$. Hence all join states on this adiabat over fixed $v_1$ lie in one thermal class. Fixing a second-component work coordinate instead gives the corresponding conclusion for first components. [A2, F4, step 3.1]

5.1 Let $\Omega$ be the open connected work-coordinate projection of $\partial A_\phi$ from [F4]. From any point of $\Omega$, the set reachable by finitely many coordinate-axis segments contained in open boxes in $\Omega$ is relatively open, and its complement is also relatively open; connectedness makes the reachable set all of $\Omega$. Along each such segment, step 4.1 gives equivalence of the corresponding join states; T3 composes these finitely many equivalences. Thus the whole adiabat $\partial A_\phi$ is one thermal class. Since the argument works for every starting join state, every join adiabat is one thermal class. [A2, F4, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Still assuming no calibrator, apply [F3] to each join system. Its alternative with two thermally inequivalent states on one adiabat is excluded by step 5.1, so all states of each join system are thermally equivalent. For any $x,x'\in\Gamma_1$, use T5 with one allowed second work coordinate to choose $y,y'$ with $x\sim_T y$ and $x'\sim_T y'$. C1 relates each component to its joined state, and all join states are in one thermal class; T3 therefore gives $x\sim_T x'$. The same argument gives one thermal class in $\Gamma_2$. Now take $Z=\phi\in\partial A_\phi$ and a split $(x,y)$ supplied by T2. Choose nonzero sufficiently small $\delta$ so $(u_x+\delta,v_1)\in\Gamma_1$ and $(u_y-\delta,v_2)\in\Gamma_2$, possible because the domains are open. These states form a distinct split of the same $Z$. Since the original split has $x\sim_T y$ and each component type is one thermal class, T3 gives thermal equivalence of the changed pair as well. This contradicts uniqueness of the split from step 2.1. Therefore a calibrator exists. [A2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 5.1, choose]

7.1 Fix a calibrator $x_0\prec\prec x_1$, $y_0\prec\prec y_1$, whose existence is step 6.1. Choose same-type entropy representatives $S_1,S_2$ from [F2], with positive gaps $h_1=S_1(x_1)-S_1(x_0)$ and $h_2=S_2(y_1)-S_2(y_0)$. Normalize $\widetilde S_i=S_i/h_i$, so both calibrator increments are one, and put $s(x)=\widetilde S_1(x)-\widetilde S_1(x_0)$ and $t(y)=\widetilde S_2(y)-\widetilde S_2(y_0)$. Write $u=\iota(x_0)+\iota(y_1)$ and $v=\iota(x_1)+\iota(y_0)$. The calibrator says $u\sim v$, so $v-u=(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))-(\iota(y_1)-\iota(y_0))$ is equivalent to zero; translation and cancellation [F5] give $(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))\sim_s(\iota(y_1)-\iota(y_0))$. For any state $x$, the signed map $d_x=\iota(x)-(1-s(x))\iota(x_0)-s(x)\iota(x_1)$ has total mass and $\widetilde S_1$-value zero. Its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy, so [F2] makes them equivalent. Hence $\iota(x)\sim_s(1-s(x))\iota(x_0)+s(x)\iota(x_1)$; the same argument applies to states of the second type. These are formal signed maps when a coefficient lies outside $[0,1]$. [F2, F5, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 For a state pair $(x,y)$, put $\lambda=(s(x)+t(y))/2$ and $\delta=(s(x)-t(y))/2$. Adding the signed reductions from step 7.1 makes the pair equivalent to $(1-\lambda)(\iota(x_0)+\iota(y_0))+\lambda(\iota(x_1)+\iota(y_1))$ plus $\delta[(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))-(\iota(y_1)-\iota(y_0))]$. The calibrator increment equivalence from step 7.1 makes the latter term equivalent to zero for either sign of $\delta$. Thus each pair reduces to its reference map at parameter $\lambda$. For any finite compound $A$ with amounts $M_1,M_2$ of the two types, add and scale these single-state reductions. Writing $q_1(A),q_2(A)$ for the amount-weighted sums of $s(x),t(y)$, respectively, gives $A\sim_s(M_1-q_1(A))\iota(x_0)+q_1(A)\iota(x_1)+(M_2-q_2(A))\iota(y_0)+q_2(A)\iota(y_1)$. Using $(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))\sim_s(\iota(y_1)-\iota(y_0))$, this is equivalent to $M_1\iota(x_0)+M_2\iota(y_0)+Q(A)(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))$, where $Q(A)=q_1(A)+q_2(A)$. If the total mass is zero, both compounds are empty and reflexivity compares them. Otherwise, for same-composition $A,B$, their base terms agree. If $Q(A)<Q(B)$, the positive and negative parts of the reference-map difference are $(Q(B)-Q(A))\iota(x_1)$ and $(Q(B)-Q(A))\iota(x_0)$, so $x_0\prec x_1$ and positive scaling compares the maps forward. If the Q values agree the maps coincide; if $Q(A)>Q(B)$ the reverse comparison holds. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F5] transfer the result to $A,B$. This proves CH for every fixed finite composition of the two types and their scaled copies. [A1, F2, F5, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph.title: Forward orientation and the Lipschitz boundary graph

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorems 3.3–3.5, pp. 45–47
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.1 and 7.2–7.3, complete 607-page edition

thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph.statement:
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.
thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F10]. Write a support plane's inward unit normal with energy component nonzero, as ensured by its finite-slope form.

1.1 For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side. [A1, F1, F4]

1.2 The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant. [A1, F2, F3, F4]

1.3 Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain. [A1, F6, F8, F9, F10, given, construct]

2.1 The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. The nested compact intervals have a common limit point $x_\infty\in\Gamma_i$ by [F7], and their lengths tend to zero. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side. [A1, F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$. [step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

5.1 Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 4.1]

6.1 For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative. [A1, F1, F5, step 5.1]

7.1 If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$. [A1, F1, step 6.1, step 1.3] ∎

thm-tdmath-reaction-offset-feasibility.title: Feasibility of finite reaction offsets

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B
Stanford EE464, Fourier–Motzkin Elimination lecture notes

thm-tdmath-reaction-offset-feasibility.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of reaction channels, let $r\in\mathbb N$, let $\nu_a\in\mathbb R^r$ be the output-minus-input type vector of channel $a$, and let $d_a\in\mathbb R$ be a finite lower bound on its already calibrated entropy change. There exists an offset vector $b\in\mathbb R^r$ satisfying

$$b\cdot\nu_a+d_a\ge0\qquad(a\in A)$$

if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^A$ with $\lambda_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a\nu_a=0$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. If an actual transition has entropy change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, such a vector guarantees $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge0$. The criterion is exact for the finite lower-bound inequalities; it does not claim necessity for actual transitions when $d_a$ is only a loose bound.
thm-tdmath-reaction-offset-feasibility.proof:
**Given:** [A1] and [F1].

1.1 Apply [F1] to the rows $c_a=
u_a$ and $h_a=-d_a$. The row system $
u_a\cdot b\ge-d_a$ is exactly the required offset system. Its multiplier condition is $\sum_a\lambda_a
u_a=0\Rightarrow\sum_a\lambda_a(-d_a)\le0$, which is equivalent to $\sum_a\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. This proves the if-and-only-if, including $A=\varnothing$ where $b=0$ is feasible and the multiplier condition is vacuous. If $r=0$ and $A$ is nonempty, every $
u_a=0$; testing the coordinate multiplier for each channel makes the criterion equivalent to $d_a\ge0$ for every $a$, and then the unique empty vector $b$ satisfies all rows. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For any channel with actual change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, add $b\cdot
u_a$ to both sides of that bound and use the solved row inequality $b\cdot
u_a\ge-d_a$. Then $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot
u_a\ge d_a+b\cdot
u_a\ge0$. This is a sufficient monotonicity conclusion for the stated channels. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing.title: Reference-strip gluing proves comparison for scaled copies

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 4.4 and Lemma 4.1, pp. 54–56
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing.statement: Assume [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and T1–T4 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] for every finite join. For any one simple type $\Gamma_i$, every two finite compounds of its scaled copies with the same total coefficient mass are comparable. Thus CH holds on all multiple scaled products of that type. No entropy across different material types is asserted here.
thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing.proof:
1.1 By T4, the open strips $\Sigma(a,b):=\{x:a\prec\prec x\prec\prec b\}$ with $a\prec\prec b$ and $a\sim_T b$ cover $\Gamma_i$. They are open: by [F2], $a\prec\prec x$ is $x\in\operatorname{int}A_a$, and $x\prec\prec b$ is $x\notin A_b$; the latter set is open because $A_b$ is relatively closed. [A1, A2, F2]

1.2 Let $\Sigma(a,b)$ and $\Sigma(c,d)$ overlap. Their intersection is open. Choose two states $e\prec\prec f$ in a small vertical segment contained in the overlap, using [F4]. Let $s_e,s_f$ be their coordinates in the first strip and $t_e,t_f$ in the second, supplied by [F1]. If $s_f<s_e$, the signed difference $R_{s_e}-R_{s_f}=(s_e-s_f)(\iota(b)-\iota(a))$ and positive scaling and signed compatibility [A1, F3] give $R_{s_f}\prec R_{s_e}$, so $f\prec e$ by the two reference equivalences; if $s_f=s_e$, those references coincide and give $f\sim e$. Both contradict $e\prec\prec f$. Hence $s_f>s_e$, and the same argument gives $t_f>t_e$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 The four reference equivalences give, in signed comparison,
$f-e\sim_s(s_f-s_e)(b-a),\qquad f-e\sim_s(t_f-t_e)(d-c).$
Put $r=(s_f-s_e)/(t_f-t_e)>0$. Additivity and positive scaling in [F3] give $d-c\sim_s r(b-a)$. Applying the same algebra to the equivalences for $e$ gives $c\sim_s a+(s_e-r t_e)(b-a)$. Consequently a state in the second strip with coordinate $t$ has first-chart coordinate $s_e+r(t-t_e)$. The change of chart is affine with strictly positive slope. [F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The same calculation covers a finite chain of overlapping strips: after each overlap, express the new strip's endpoint states as signed-equivalent affine maps in the existing reference pair. The local strip lemma gives every state $z$ of the added strip a coordinate $s_z\in\mathbb R$ with $\iota(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\iota(a)+s_z\iota(b)$ in the existing chart. Signed addition, positive scaling, translation, and equivalence under negative scaling are valid by [F3]; hence induction along a finite overlap chain gives one such common chart for every state in the union. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Take any finite list of target states in $\Gamma_i$ and join them in order by finitely many straight segments, which lie in $\Gamma_i$ by convexity. The resulting connected path is a finite union of closed bounded segments, hence compact by [F5]. The open strips from step 1.1 cover it, so compactness gives a finite subcover. The intersection graph of those strips meeting the path is connected: otherwise their unions would partition the connected path into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Order a spanning tree from one root strip; each later strip overlaps an earlier one in an open set and can be glued by step 3.1. Thus every target state has a common signed chart $\iota(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\iota(a)+s_z\iota(b)$ with $a\prec\prec b$. [A1, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Let $A=\sum_j\alpha_j \iota(x_j)$ and $B=\sum_k\beta_k \iota(y_k)$ have equal total mass $M$, and let $s_j,t_k$ be their common-chart coordinates. If $M=0$, nonnegativity makes both maps empty and reflexivity compares them. Assume $M>0$ and put $L:=M/w_{\Gamma_i}$; both sums of scalar amounts are $L$, since each represented state has mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$. Each state has signed equivalence $\iota(x_j)\sim_s(1-s_j)\iota(a)+s_j\iota(b)$ in the common chart; signed addition, scaling, and splitting [F3] therefore make $A$ and $B$ each signed-equivalent to reference maps $R_{q_A}=(L-q_A)\iota(a)+q_A\iota(b)$ and $R_{q_B}=(L-q_B)\iota(a)+q_B\iota(b)$, where $q_A=\sum_j\alpha_js_j$ and $q_B=\sum_k\beta_kt_k$. If $q_A<q_B$, the signed difference has positive part $(q_B-q_A)\iota(b)$ and negative part $(q_B-q_A)\iota(a)$, so $a\prec b$ and positive scaling compare $R_{q_A}\prec R_{q_B}$ by [F3]. If $q_A=q_B$, the reference maps coincide and reflexivity applies; if $q_B<q_A$, the same argument compares in the reverse direction. Transitivity transfers that comparison to $A,B$. Hence any equal-mass pair is comparable, proving CH. [A1, F3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-sector-nesting.title: Nesting and comparison of simple-system states

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorems 3.6–3.8, pp. 47–50
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.1 and 7.2–7.3, complete 607-page edition

thm-tdmath-sector-nesting.statement: Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.
thm-tdmath-sector-nesting.proof:
1.1 If $y\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x$. If also $y\in\partial A_x$, [F3] gives equality. Suppose instead $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. If $A_y$ met $\partial A_x$ at $z$, then $z\in A_y$ and [F3] would give $A_z=A_x$. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y\subseteq A_x$, so $A_y=A_x$.
