But S2 puts $y$ on $\partial A_y$, contradicting $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. Thus $A_y$ avoids $\partial A_x$ and, being a subset of the closed sector $A_x$, lies in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. [A1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Suppose neither $y\in A_x$ nor $x\in A_y$. Choose $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ using [F2]. The segment from $y$ to $z$ lies in $\Gamma_i$ and meets $\partial A_x$ at a point $w$ strictly between its endpoints. By [F3], $A_w=A_x$, so $w\prec z$. The collinear implication in [F1], applied to $w=ty+(1-t)z$, gives $y\prec w\prec z$. Hence every $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ lies in $A_y$. Reversing $x,y$ gives $\operatorname{int}A_y\subseteq A_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Because $A_x$ is full-dimensional by [F2], its affine hull is the ambient space. Fix $w\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. For any $q\in A_x$, relative closedness gives $q\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$, and [F4] puts $(1-t)w+tq$ in $\operatorname{int}A_x$ for every $0\le t<1$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ shows $q\in\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. The reverse inclusion follows because $A_x$ is relatively closed. Hence $A_x=\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$; the same holds for $A_y$. Relative closedness from [F1] therefore extends the two interior inclusions in step 1.2 to $A_x\subseteq A_y$ and $A_y\subseteq A_x$. Equality would put $x\in A_y$, contradicting the supposition. Thus at least one of $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ always holds. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 If $x\prec y$, then $y\in A_x$. If $y$ is a boundary point, step 1.1 gives $A_x=A_y$, hence $x\prec y$ and $y\prec x$. Otherwise step 1.1 gives $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}A_x$, and $x\notin A_y$ because S2 places $x$ on $\partial A_x$. Thus $x\prec\prec y$. Conversely, if $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$, step 1.1 and S2 show $x\notin A_y$, so $x\prec\prec y$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-splitting-cost-quotient.title: No-sinks cost offsets give a weak global entropy

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B, pp. 76–80

thm-tdmath-splitting-cost-quotient.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $F$ be the decorated cost of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], and assume the **no-sinks condition**

$$F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F(\Gamma',\Gamma)<+\infty$$

for every type pair. Let $V_F$ be the real difference space of [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]]. Then there is an additive extensive offset $B:\mathcal G\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$-F(\Gamma',\Gamma)\le B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma').$$

If every admitted cross-type transition $x\prec y$ from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ satisfies the calibrated cost inequality of [[thm-tdmath-unattained-cost-entropy-inference]], then $\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)$ is nondecreasing across every such transition. Only this weak inequality is asserted; no-gap equalities and strict extensions are not concluded.
thm-tdmath-splitting-cost-quotient.proof:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F4], and the no-sinks condition.

1.1 If $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty$, no-sinks gives a finite reverse witness of some real cost $c$. Concatenating it with any forward witness makes a closed chain, so [F2] gives forward cost at least $-c$. Thus $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')>-\infty$ whenever it is finite; all cost values are in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. [A1, F2, given]

2.1 For a pair class $v=[\Gamma,\Gamma']\in V_F$, define $p(v):=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Suppose $(\Gamma,\Gamma')\equiv(\Lambda,\Lambda')$ via $C$, so $P=\Gamma\times\Lambda'\times C\approx_0 Q=\Lambda\times\Gamma'\times C$. Put $D=\Gamma'\times\Lambda'\times C$. Since $P\approx_0 Q$, the triangle inequality gives $F(P,D)\le F(Q,D)$ and $F(Q,D)\le F(P,D)$; the costs have no $-\infty$ by step 1.1, so these inequalities imply equality. Catalyst invariance from [F2] gives $F(P,D)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ and $F(Q,D)=F(\Lambda,\Lambda')$. Therefore $p$ is independent of the pair representative. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The identity $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$ gives $p(0)=0$. Homogeneity of $F$ gives $p(tv)=tp(v)$ for $t>0$, and its product subadditivity gives $p(v+w)\le p(v)+p(w)$. The no-sinks condition says $p(v)<+\infty$ exactly when $p(-v)<+\infty$. By step 1.1, $p$ has no $-\infty$ value. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply [F3] to $V_F$ and $p$. It gives a real-linear $L:V_F\to\mathbb R$ with $-p(-v)\le L(v)\le p(v)$ for all $v$. Put $B(\Gamma)=L([\Gamma,1])$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. Since $[\Gamma\times\Gamma',1]=[\Gamma,1]+[\Gamma',1]$, $B$ is additive. Since $[t\Gamma,1]=t[\Gamma,1]$ (the unit type satisfies $t1=1$), $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$. Also $[\Gamma,\Gamma']=[\Gamma,1]-[\Gamma',1]$, so applying the sandwich to this pair gives the displayed two-sided cost bound. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For an admitted transition, [F4] gives $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, while step 3.1 gives $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Subtracting the latter from the former yields
$[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)+B(\Gamma')]-[\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)]\ge0.$
Thus the offset entropy is nondecreasing across every admitted transition. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

thm-tdmath-unattained-cost-entropy-infer.title: Catalyst-chain cost characterizes cross-type transitions

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 6.1 and proof, pp. 75–76
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapters 2 and 4, complete 607-page edition

thm-tdmath-unattained-cost-entropy-infer.statement:
Assume the calibrated entropy family of [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]], the cross-type accessibility axioms A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and the decorated cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]. For every pair of types $\Gamma,\Gamma'$ and states $x\in X_\Gamma$, $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$,

$$x\prec y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_\Gamma(x)+F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le \sigma_{\Gamma'}(y).$$

The infimum defining $F$ need not be attained. If $F=+\infty$, the right side is false; if $F=-\infty$, the right side is true.
thm-tdmath-unattained-cost-entropy-infer.proof:
1.1 If $x\prec y$, the one-edge witness with an identity catalyst has cost $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$. Hence $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$, which is the forward inequality, including the case $F=+\infty$ where no such transition can exist. [F1, F2]

1.2 Conversely assume the displayed entropy inequality. It is impossible when $F=+\infty$. For each integer $n\ge1$, choose a decorated witness of real cost $c_n\le\Delta\sigma+h/n$, where $\Delta\sigma=\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$ and $h=\sigma(z_1)-\sigma(z_0)>0$ is the entropy gap of a fixed strict meter pair from [F1]. Such witnesses exist from the definition of infimum, also if $F=-\infty$. Write their types as $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, their edges as $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$, and their endpoints as $a_0=(\widetilde x,c_0)$, $b_N=(\widetilde y,d_0)$. [F1, F2, F3, choose]

2.1 Put $\delta_n=1/n$. In one finite compound type form
$L_n=(x,b_N,b_1,\ldots,b_{N-1},\delta_n z_0),\qquad R_n=(a_0,y,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1},\delta_n z_1).$
These have the same composition: both contain $\Gamma$, $\Gamma'$, the catalyst $C$, every intermediate type $T_1,\ldots,T_{N-1}$, and one scaled meter state, up to reassociation and permutation. Additivity of $\sigma$ and the definition of chain cost give
$\sigma(R_n)-\sigma(L_n)=\Delta\sigma-c_n+\delta_n h\ge0.$
Thus the same-composition entropy representation [F1] gives $L_n\prec R_n$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Starting from $R_n$, use consistency on $a_0\prec b_1$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators. The result contains $b_1$ in place of $a_0$. Next use $a_1\prec b_2$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,b_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators, and continue in order. At stage $k$, the current compound contains $a_k$, the earlier outputs $b_1,\ldots,b_k$, all later inputs $a_{k+1},\ldots,a_{N-1}$, and the unchanged $y,\delta_nz_1$. After the last edge, transitivity gives $R_n\prec R'_n$, where $R'_n=(b_1,\ldots,b_N,y,\delta_nz_1)$. Compose this with $L_n\prec R_n$ from step 2.1. The compounds $L_n$ and $R'_n$ share the finite spectator $b_1+\cdots+b_N$; cancel it by [F4]. The result is $x+\delta_nz_0\prec y+\delta_nz_1$ for every $n$. [A1, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $\delta_n\downarrow0$, stability in [A1] with bases $x,y$ and fixed positive spectators $z_0,z_1$ yields $x\prec y$. This proves the reverse implication without assuming that any infimum is attained. [A1, step 3.1] ∎

cex-td-degenerate-thermometer-comparison.title: Degenerate thermometers can fail product comparison

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §IV.C, pp. 59–60
André Thess, The Lieb–Yngvason Machine: A didactical tool for the definition of entropy in classical thermodynamics, §2
Goddard, The second law of thermodynamics as variation on a theme of Carathéodory, §3

cex-td-degenerate-thermometer-comparison.statement: The one-system order relation $U\le U'$ on a degenerate thermometer state space $\Gamma=(0,\infty)$, together with the thermal equilibration operation described below, need not satisfy T4 or the comparison hypothesis on products. Consequently, a monotone entropy on the single-system space need not represent product accessibility.
cex-td-degenerate-thermometer-comparison.proof:
**Given:** [F1]–[F2] and the product sector specified above.

1.1 Start at $(1,3)$. Then $\bar U=2$, every point of $A$ has second coordinate at least $3$, and every point of $B$ has second coordinate at least $2$. A finite convex combination of points whose second coordinates are at least $2$ still has second coordinate at least $2$, because it is the weighted sum of those coordinates with nonnegative weights summing to one. Hence every point in $\operatorname{conv}(A\cup B)$ has second coordinate at least $2$, so $(3,1)$ is not in the forward sector and $(1,3)\not\prec(3,1)$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 In the one-system space, strict accessibility is exactly strict increase of $U$, while thermal equilibrium is equality of normalized energies. If $U_0\prec\prec U\prec\prec U_1$, then $U_0<U<U_1$, so $U_0\ne U_1$ and the two cannot be thermally equivalent. Thus T4 fails. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Start instead at $(3,1)$. Again $\bar U=2$; every point of its $A$ has first coordinate at least $3$, and every point of its $B$ has first coordinate at least $2$. Convex combinations therefore have first coordinate at least $2$, so $(1,3)$ is not accessible from $(3,1)$. The two product states are incomparable, and the comparison hypothesis fails. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The single-system function $S(U)=\log U$ is strictly increasing and represents $U\le U'$. If its additive sum represented product accessibility, the states $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$ would have equal summed entropy $\log 3$, forcing accessibility both ways. Step 1.1 and step 2.1 show neither direction holds. Therefore this single-system entropy does not represent the product relation. Since the example fails T4 by step 1.2, it does not satisfy the hypotheses of a product-comparison result that includes T4. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
cex-td-degenerate-thermometer-comparison.physical_scope: An abstract positive-energy thermometer model showing failure of T4 and the comparison hypothesis for products; it is not a measured thermometer or a claim about ordinary thermodynamic bodies.

ex-tdmath-reaction-offset-cycle-obstruct.title: A two-channel cycle obstructs reaction offsets

references.title: Stanford EE464, Fourier–Motzkin Elimination lecture notes

ex-tdmath-reaction-offset-cycle-obstruct.proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[F2].

1.1 The multiplier $\lambda=(1,1)$ is nonnegative and satisfies $\lambda_1\nu_1+\lambda_2\nu_2=(1,-1)+(-1,1)=(0,0)$. But $\lambda_1d_1+\lambda_2d_2=-2+1=-1<0$, violating the necessary condition in [F1]; therefore no offset exists. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Directly, the two inequalities would require $b_1-b_2\ge2$ and $-b_1+b_2\ge-1$, equivalently $b_1-b_2\le1$. Adding the original inequalities gives $0\ge1$, a contradiction. This is the positive-right-side zero-left certificate of [F2]. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
